Answering further my right hon. friend's question as to the meaning of other assistance, in the provincial legislation "supplies" means petroleum products, feed grain, fodder, repairs to implements and parts, formaldehyde and gopher poison, and includes such other commodities and such services as the lieutenant governor in oouncil may approve. It has to do entirely with seeding, but apparently the word requires a fairly broad definition.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
The reason I desired that question to be answered Mr. Chairman, was to ascertain what assurance there would be that everyone would be dealt with fairly and on the same basis. I am not imputing motives to anyone, but I may say that I have received communications during the last few years as to administrative activities in connection with the distribution of assistance, on the one hand, and with the purchasing of hay, we will say, on the other, for purposes of feed. What assurance is there that there will be no favourites selected in the distribution of this assistance for seeding? It is a matter of first rate practical importance. It is all right to say that the municipalities have to deal with it, but by reason of their present position the municipalities
have become to some extent the controlled creatures, more or less, of provincial governments, and if the municipalities are to make distribution at the caprice of the reeve or whoever the official may be, great difficulty might be experienced by those who were rightly entitled to>
this relief. It is not a mere suggestion that this might happen, because it has happened.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
It is difficult to see how
we can go back of the responsibility of an organized municipality operated by its own responsible elected officers. I may say also that the legislation provides for the necessary by-law and sets out the form of it. The municipality is the borrower of the money. The taxpayers of the municipalities are initially responsible for it, and therein lies our protection, I think, against any abuse. Certainly the dominion government cannot contemplate going into every rural municipality to ensure that discrimination does not take place in a matter which after all is initially a responsibility of the municipality under provincial legislation, and secondly is the responsibility of the province by virtue of its guarantee, and the responsibility of the province in a more important sense because it undertakes to reimburse the dominion in respect of any sums which the dominion may have to pay ultimately under the terms of its guarantee. While I appreciate as much as the leader of the opposition the desirability and necessity of avoiding discrimination in the distribution of seed grain under this legislation, I cannot see how it is possible for the dominion to undertake to ensure that there will not be any; but knowing the men as I do-for I have some knowledge of the men elected as rural municipal councillors and reeves in the province of Saskatchewan-I do not think we need be apprehensive of discrimination. Of course public men always will hear-I do and I am sure my right hon. friend does- from those who for good reasons have been refused by their neighbours the accommodation required, and who always allege discrimination for political or other reasons. I have received communications, as has my right hon. friend, and there may be some foundation for them in some cases. However, I doubt if we can go back of the responsibility which rests upon the elected representatives of the people of the municipality when utilizing the municipalities' and taxpayers' money or credit for the purpose of dealing with this matter.

speechtext:
1930 wheat crop
Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 22, to provide for the payment of certain sums of money to primary producers of wheat with respect to wheat of the 1930 crop delivered to provincial pool organizations.
He said: This'bill, which was preceded by the resolution discussed during the last two or three days, is an extraordinary measure, brought before the house because of extraordinary conditions. It is unusual for the house to be called upon to provide for payment in connection with a crop grown and marketed or partly marketed five years ago. Because of the extraordinary nature of the claims made in connection with that crop and the handling of the question down to the present the bill itself is of an extraordinary nature. There is a rather long preamble, in which the government have set forth in detailed form the reasons for taking this extraordinary action. There is, in addition to the nature of the problem itself, another reason for bringing down this measure, it is that no authority was given in the legislation of last year to deal with certain matters that the government think ought to be dealt with, and even touching that part of the crop of 1930 for which some legal provision had been made in the legislation of last session, there are reasons for dealing with it by legislation in order that a full discussion of this extraordinary state of affairs should be before the country and before the house when a vote is taken on the question. I say, "before the country," because of the many rumours that have gone out in connection with the payment, the rather wide discussion as to whether the crop should be paid for or whether payments in addition to those already made should be made in connection with the crop at this or at any other time. Then, again I think, because of the extraordinary nature of the conditions necessitating this legislation, and the nature of the legislation itself, the house should have a full understanding of the surrounding conditions.
Western Canada, as is generally known, and well known in this house from the discussions we have been carrying on this afternoon and on previous occasions, is preeminently a grain growing section. The growing of grain in that part of the country is surrounded by difficult conditions. One is the fact that it is so far north, another that being so far north it is essential to the growing of grain there at all that we have the kind

of climate that, generally speaking, we do have in western Canada. But the condition which more than any other concerns the passing of this legislation is the fact that this grain growing section is located in the centre of a continent, a long distance from ports from which the grain can be shipped, and thousands of miles from the markets where the greater part of the grain is sold and consumed. This latter condition brings to the dealing with wheat in particular, and other grains to a lesser degree, a considerable risk. That risk arises from the distance of the wheat fields from the markets, and the time that elapsed between the harvesting of the crop the milling of the wheat into flour and the consumption of it in Europe.
Because of the element of chance that enters into the marketing of the grain it was considered necessary in the early days of grain growing in western Canada to set up a system of options. That system of options has to do to some extent with the carrying of the risk assumed by those who take over the grain in the first place from the farmers, hold it during the time it may be held in Canada, and eventually market it in Europe. Ever since that system was first set up there has been a great deal of controversy between the producers of the crop and the initial handlers of it as it passes from the fields of production to where it is to be consumed.
The organization set up in Winnipeg to take care of these dealings was the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, and usually when we are critical of the handing of our grain the criticism is directed at the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. As a result of the criticisms that took place over a term of years efforts were made on the part of the farmers to set up organizations of one kind and another to gain greater control over the marketing of their crop. The first real effort to get control of the marketing of the crops was embodied in a bill passed by this house many years ago and entitled the Canada Grain Act, by which many safeguards were placed about the trade in the interests of the producers.
In more recent times the efforts of the producers took the form of building up a cooperative organization. The final effort made in that connection was in 1923 and continued into 1924. That effort was to build up a contract pool; that is, the farmers of western Canada were asked to sign a contract that they would deliver their wheat to a pool organization for a five year period. And I may say that so many were convinced that this method was superior to that followed previously that over fifty per cent of the farmers of Saskatchewan, over fifty per cent

Wheat Board-Mr. Gardiner
of the farmers of Alberta and over forty per cent of the farmers of Manitoba signed that contract in the years 1923 and 1924. In so far as Saskatchewan is concerned, between that time and five years later the percentage of those signing the contract had been increased to sixty per cent of all the farmers in the province. A second sign-up was made in 1929, and in Saskatchewan sixty-five per cent of the farmers signed the renewed contract, which would indicate that at that time they had considerable confidence in the organization that had been set up.
May I say that the wheat pool was set up for the purpose of carrying those risks that had previously 'been carried through the buying and selling of options, what we are pleased to call speculation in grain, guessing as to what the price would- be by the time the grain reached the market where it was going to be consumed. The wheat pool- was set up for the purpose of overcoming the necessity of having that element of speculation in the grain trade, and the method by which this was to be accomplished was, according to those who advocated that system, to have the farmer carry his own risks. He delivered his wheat to the organization and received an initial payment; if the price received1 for the wheat during the season was sufficient he received an interim payment during the season, and at the end of it he received his final payment- of the amount that had been obtained for the grain. That system, I repeat, was intended to provide a means whereby the farmer carried his own risks. If the price went up he secured more. If the price went down it was intended that provision would be made for the financing of the grain to be taken care of without anyone else being called upon to provide funds.
For some years, from 1924 to 1928, there was no difficulty in operating the pooling method of handling grain. During those years we had either a rising price or a fairly stable price for wheat, and there was very little difficulty in having that wheat delivered to the pool organizations, delivered ' by the pool organizations to the central' selling agency, known as the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, with offices at Winnipeg, sent on to the markets of the world and marketed, with interim payments and final payments being made later on as a result of the selling of the crop.
But difficulty arose in the year 1928. That difficulty arose because prices of wheat began to go down. I think any member of this house who is familiar with the marketing of any commodity, more particularly the marketing of wheat, will agree with me that if any 12739-981
system of handling products, and more especially wheat, is going to be successful for the farmers of western Canada, it will have to be a system that is capable of handling that wheat while prices are going down as well as while prices are rising or remaining more or less stable. In 1928 difficulties were experienced. In 1929 greater difficulties were experienced. The greater difficulties of 1929 arose out of this fact, that an initial price of one dollar a bushel was set for wheat, and wheat went down between the time it was harvested and the following summer from $1.73 to eighty-six cents a bushel.
The conditions under which the financing of the pools had been- done by the banks provided that there was always to be maintained a margin of fifteen cents between- the initial price paid, and the price that was actually being obtained for the wheat. When the price got down to about $1.26, or within eleven cents of the margin which the banks had set, the banks began to insist upon payment of the amounts of money that had been advanced to the pools, and when that insistence took -place the pools were face to face with the question whether they were going to sell their wheat and obtain the money or whether they would ask someone to assist them in financing through their period of difficulty. They chose the latter course. They went to the three provincial governments of western Canada, and asked those three provincial governments to guarantee the banks against losses in connection with financing the crop of 1929-30, and the sale of the carry-over from the crop of 1928. The three provincial governments undertook to do so, and they gave their guarantee against loss to the financing banks. That guarantee was made effective through legislation passed in the legislatures of the three western provinces; the pools went on to pay a price of one dollar a bushel during that season, and let me repeat, by the end of the season the price was eighty-six cents a bushel, although at the beginning of the season it had been $1.73.
At the end of the 1929 crop year the wheat pools had a carry-over of 43,000,000 bushels. Now, it was intended and expected at the beginning -of the organization of the pools that they wo-uld be able to market the crop from year to year, feeding it to the market regularly, as was said at that time, and that at the end of the year all the money that was available as a result of the sale of the crop would be paid out in a final payment to the farmers. But at the end of the 1929 crop year, in the middle of 1930, there was a carry-over of 43,000,000 bushels of wheat.

Wheat Board-Mr. Gardiner
I have recited 'these facts, Mr. Speaker, only to point out to the house that until the end of the 1929 crop year the federal government had no liability in connection with any operations having to do with the pooling of wheat. During the first four years of the operations of the pools the liability in connection with the wheat was carried successfully by the farmers. During the next year the governments of the three western provinces were assisting by giving their guarantee, and may I say that as a result of giving that guarantee the three western provinces, which eventually had to implement the guarantee, are carrying or were carrying in the neighbourhood of $25,000,000 as a result of losses incurred in connection with the marketing of that year's crop. All this experience was before the Dominion of Canada, and more particularly before western Canada, in the year 1929 and until July 31, 1930, which is the end of the pool crop year.
About the end of July, 1930, there were two or three events of importance. There was an election in July and a change of government on the seventh day of August. Two or three days before the government changed, I think on the fifth of August, representatives of the pools and, I believe, too, representatives of the provincial governments, came to eastern Canada for the purpose of trying to make arrangements for the financing of the 1930 crop. I understand that the first interviews with the government were between the ninth and twelfth of August, a few days after the government changed. Just prior to these negotiations, on July 16, the pools had set an initial price of seventy cents a bushel for the wheat crop of 1930. Admittedly that was only an interim price, set to meet conditions at the beginning of the season before any crop had come on to the market. This did not involve any arrangements with the banks or with the governments in connection with the new crop.
When these representatives came to Ottawa and met the government on different occasions between the ninth and twelfth of August there were discussions with regard to the financing of the 1930 crop. On August 26, as a result of discussions with the banks, with the provincial governments and with the federal government a price of sixty cents per bushel was agreed upon as the initial price to be paid by the pools for the crop of 1930. That initial price of sixty cents carried with it an understanding between the banks, the governments and the pools as to how any losses might be met, but no publicity was given to any of the understandings reached at that

particular time other than an intimation that at that early date the federal government was not prepared to guarantee the losses of the banks in connection with the crop.
Further negotiations were carried on until the month of October as the price of wheat was going down all the time. In October the initial price was reduced to fifty-five cents a bushel, basis No. 1 northern, Fort William. The price of wheat still continued to go down and changes occurred in the initial price to agree with the fifteen cent margin given to the banks. Eveiy time the initial price of wheat came down past that fifteen cent margin it was necessary to set a new initial price. The first reduction was from seventy to sixty cents a bushel, the second from sixty to fifty-five cents and the third from fifty-five cents to fifty cents, which was made in November, 1930.
It might be of interest to hon. members to know what the price of wheat was on those different dates. These prices are contained in the report of the auditors tabled the other day in committee. The set price of seventy cents a bushel was put into effect when wheat was selling at 95|- cents a bushel, on July 16, 1930. The set price of sixty cents a bushel was put into effect when wheat was selling at 85f cents a bushel, on August 26. The set price of fifty-five cents was put into effect when wheat was selling at 72i cents a bushel, on October 15. On November 11 the set price was fifty cents when wheat was selling at 65| cents a bushel. There are two points that should be noted in connection with these prices and the reductions in the initial price. There was a margin of twenty-five cents a bushel when the seventy cent a bushel initial price was set. When the price came down to eighty-eight cents they were within eighteen cents of the margin, and the price was reduced to sixty cents. When it came down to 72& cents a bushel they were 2J cents below the margin and the price was reduced to fifty-five cents a bushel. When it got down to 65| cents, they were 4f cents a bushel below the margin, and the price was reduced to fifty cents.
The second important point to be remembered is the fact that from July 16 to November 11 the price remained above sixty cents a bushel. During that period usually about seventy per cent of the crop of western Canada passes out of the hands of the farmers into the hands of those who handle the grain. In other words, approximately seventy per cent of the grain was actually marketed at a price above sixty cents per bushel. Those who sold outside the pools obtained over sixty cents per bushel if they sold outright, or at least

Wheat Board-Mr. Gardiner
on the basis of sixty cents per bushel. I have the exact figures of what was marketed through the pools in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan, and they show the same proportion that I am speaking of in connection with the whole crop.
With these facts in mind I think we should give some consideration to the time when the federal government began to assume some relationship in a financial way to the activities of the pools, and hence towards the marketing of grain from the western part of Canada. Further than that, the Argentina had actually decreased its wheat acreage at one time before it started in to increase the area sown. We are sometimes prone to blame the Argentine for the action it has taken in forcing its wheat upon the markets of the world at a low figure.
The whole trend of this speech at this point is to criticize the increase in acreage in the Dominion of Canada and to compare that increase with the comparatively small increase in the United States. The years selected for the comparison are those from 1909 to 1913 for the first figure and 1933 for the comparative figure. Every member of this house who has been following the situation in connection with wheat knows that prior to the war the United States had reached the point at which it did not pay them to sow more acreage to wheat. Even prior to the war they were encouraging their people to go into the sowing of crops other than wheat. During the war they, like Canada, set up a board and put it to work to increase the wheat acreage. Immediately the war was over the United States set up

The wheat areas in the southwestern part of Saskatchewan and the central and eastern part of Alberta were not producing wheat in 1909 to anything like the extent they have been producing wheat since that time. As a matter of fact I think we produced only some

That has no bearing on what I am talking about at all. I am discussing pool wheat. There was a carry-over of the 1928-29 pools of 43,000,000 bushels, and that 43,000,000 bushels was disposed of as a result of arrangements made as between the provinces and the pools prior to the time the provinces implemented their guarantees given to the pools in connection with handling that wheat. On July 31, 1931, there were 76,375,000 bushels of 1930 pool wheat in the hands of Mr. McFarland; that was at the time the change was made that I said was a cut off on July 31, 1931. Now what was done with that wheat? Well, the auditor's report shows that that quantity of 76,000,000 bushels was dealt with in accordance with the policy laid down by the then Prime Minister and Mr. McFarland. It was actually taken off the market, put into an account by itself, retained in that account in order to stabilize the price to other people who were producing wheat throughout the length and breadth of Canada, and it is because these 76,000,000 bushels were taken off the market and kept off the market from 1931 to 1935 that the wheat pools have been claiming that they should have payment in connection with that wheat. The government is inclined to think their claim is well founded and that some payment should be made as a result of the fact that this wheat was taken and kept off the market, for the purpose, as the leader of the opposition would admit, whether it accomplished the purpose or not, of raising the price to other people, the same people who produced grain in other years. There is really no other ground for the claim than that.
Now, the problem that the government were then faced with was whether sixty cents was a proper price, whether we should pay the price up to a sixty cent basis. In order to determine that -we had to give consideration to certain factors. There is one thing that, in all the discussion that has taken place in connection with this matter, has not yet been explained and that I think ought to be explained; it is what I reserved my right to discuss further in connection with the order in council last evening, the question why these payments were held up for four years until the week before the election. Not even a rumour came out to the people of this country that 12739-994
any payments were going to be made in connection with the 1930 crop other than claims that were being made from time to time by representatives of the pool organization. But just while we were in the midst of the election, to be exact on October 10, 1935, rumours were published in the papers referred to last evening by the leader of the opposition. Those rumours had to do with certain statements that were made in the Winnipeg Free Press and also in the Regina Leader, but I will refer at the moment only to that made in the Winnipeg Free Press. This statement was made in an editorial on October 9:
Upon the strength of the rise in wheat prices the government stabilization agency (which is still doing business) would authorize the pool to issue cheques to pool members in adjustment of payments made on delivery of the crop in 1930-31.
Now, after having made that statement in their editorial, and having repeated, prior to writing it, these rumours going around with regard to the payment on the 1930 grain, the Free Press had their reporter interview W. A. McLeod, and W. A. McLeod's reply on October 9 was read to this house last evening. It might be well here to ask ourselves who W. A. McLeod is. Mr. W. A. McLeod is chief publicity man for Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, the gentleman who writes most of the official documents that go out from the pool in order to indicate what the pool is doing and what it is expecting. When the Free Press submitted these rumours to Mr. McLeod he is reported as having made this statement:
The Free Press Wednesday asked W. A. McLeod, prominent pool official, when these payments would be made. Mr. McLeod said there was no truth whatever in the report. "It's a damned lie," he said, "and you can tell that to whoever told the Free Press."
That statement was read just in those words by the leader of the opposition last evening, but he did not read the statement that was refuted by that remark. I have here the Western Producer, the official organ of the wheat pool, and the organ in which W. A. McLeod publishes all his publicity if he publishes it at all.

What I would like to point out to the house is that nothing has been produced to indicate that any member of the pool or any man who delivered any of that grain to_ the pool knew at that time that the government of Canada had changed the first draft of the order in council. Not a single one of them knew. And so far as the members of the house are concerned, there was not a single member who knew until yesterday that that order in council had been built up and had been signed in the manner in which it was except the men who signed it.
When these facts were brought out yesterday my right hon. friend wanted to know whether we had any idea that anything sinister had been done by the government. Well, I repeat what I said yesterday, that there was no intention on my part and no intention on the part of any member of the government to imply anything sinister in the shape of taking money out of the treasury of Canada for the benefit of any member of the government, but I have no hesitation in saying to-night that there could have been only one intention on the part of the government in holding these moneys up week after [DOT]week and month after month, yes, and in some cases year after year, after the farmers of Canada were entitled to them, and then bringing them out as an offer to the people of western Canada four days before the election. speechtext:
I said a moment ago
that there was no question, so far as the government is concerned, whether a certain amount of money should be paid in connection with the wheat. I wish now, if I am permitted to do so, to establish the amount, which we think ought to be paid, and why we think it ought to be paid. The amount claimed by the pool organization is based upon the statement which I read to the louse a few moments ago. It is based upon i statement made on February 29, 1932, at which time it is claimed that an amount of $6,509,269.36 could have been realized for distribution. They claim that is the amount to which they are entitled.

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO
speechtext: What was the then price of wheat?

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO
speechtext:
I cannot say exactly
at the moment without looking it up but it

was around sixty cents. The reasons why sixty cents is a reasonable amount to ask for are to be found in these facts. As indicated in the remarks I made this afternoon, the federal government first became interested in this matter of an initial price at the time that an initial price of sixty cents had been set. Prior to that time the federal government had not been financially interested in the wheat pools; the provincial government was carrying the load. But as a result of the first conference held by the federal government, the provincial governments and the banks, an initial price of sixty cents was set. Another reason why sixty cents might be regarded as a reasonable price is the fact that the valuation that was given the 1930 wheat, when the cut off was made on July 31, 1931, was 60J cents a bushel, and that figured out would give the amount that is proposed in the bill. Then, wheat sold at sixty cents prior to February 29, 1932, would have brought an amount in excess of the amount that is paid by the wheat pool had it been credited to the 1930 crop. In other words, there was 76,000,000 bushels of wheat sold after the federal government entered upon the guarantee. Prior to February 29,	1932 there was approximately
76.000,000 bushels of wheat sold at a price which would have brought sixty cents a bushel to the farmers had the sales been credited to the 1930 pool wheat, and what the wheat pool people claim is that it is perfectly proper that this 76,000,000 bushels should be paid for at the price that might have been realized had the 76,000.000 bushels of the 1930 crop been credited with the sales instead of being held off the market entirely and other grain sold in its place.
We might go further than that. Mr. McFarland took charge of the wheat market on July 31, 1931, and he was selling wheat over a considerable period of time. There is one period that is very interesting-July, 1933. I have before me the prices offered every day upon which wheat was sold or bought through the operations of Mr. McFarland during the month of July, 1933. I find that on July 3, 1933, the price of October wheat was 81J cents, and it runs along 82|; 81J; 82$; 83$; 84$; 86f; 90$; 90$; 93; 95; 95$; 81; 80; 75; 78; 85; 90; 83; 81; 80. It will be noted that wheat started at eighty-one cents at the first of the month, then went to ninety-five cents in the middle of the month and came back to eighty cents at the end of the month. During the first half of the month Mr. McFarland was selling wheat, and his operations resulted in a position of this kind. On June 24 he had

Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett
71.070.000	bushels of wheat; on July 3, 69,-
242,000	bushels; on July 8, 65,368,000; on July 15, 48,792,000; on July 17, 42,461,000; on July 18, 42,461,000; on July 19, 42,461,000; on July 20, 46,111,000; on July 21, 62,216,000; on July 22, 65,619,000. What were the cash prices on those dates? On June 24 the cash price was 701 cents per bushel; on July 3, 72i cents; on July 15, 95 cents and on July 22, 73| cents. What happened? On July 3, Mr. McFarland had 69,242,000 bushels of wheat. The price that day was 72J cents. He sold 1,928,000 bushels. On July 8 he sold 4,040,000 bushels; on July 15 he sold 16,545,000 bushels and on July 17, 6,333,000 bushels in his stabilization activities. He reduced the amount of wheat that he held from 69,000,000 bushels on July 3 to 42,000,000 bushels on July 17.

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO
speechtext: That is exclusive of the 1930 wheat.

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO
speechtext:
Yes, that is the other wheat; he had got the 1930 wheat off the market and he was dealing with the other wheat. What did he do after that? He did just what every man who is speculating in wheat does. For three days he sat and looked at it and it went to ninety-five cents a bushel on July 15. He sold 6,333,000 bushels on July 17, when it went down to 93i cents a bushel. He looked at it the next day and it went up one-half cent. He looked at it one day longer and it went down 6J cents. Then he thought he had better start stabilizing, so he bought 4,180,000 bushels, and wheat went down nine cents a bushel. He thought he was not stabilizing fast enough, so he bought
15.705.000	bushels, and wheat went down | cents per bushel. Then he took another try at it, so the next day he bought 3,303,000 bushels, and wheat went down 4J cents. Then he thought he had better stop for a little while. What do we find? He started out with 69,242,000 bushels and he ended up with
65.619.000	bushels.
The wheat pool people say that the average price at which wheat was sold by Mr. McFarland on the days that he sold it for future delivery in October is ninety-two cents a bushel. They say that if you take ninety-two cents a bushel for the 76,000,000 bushels of wheat that they held off the market in order to bring this about, it will give sixty cents a bushel to every farmer who delivered wheat at fifty-five or fifty cents a bushel. They say they are entitled to sixty cents per bushel.

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO
speechtext: And pay the carrying charges.

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO
speechtext:
Yes, and pay the carrying charges. They say that they are entitled to sixty cents a bushel because of the activities of Mr. McFarland during the month of July, 1933. If my right hon. friend will take the trouble to trace the activities during the summer of 1934 he will find that they are just the same. This is the man who has been so anxiously looking round for shorts in the market, but he always bought more wheat every time the market was going down then he sold when the market was going up. He had more wheat at the end of the period than he had at the beginning. At the end of July, 1934, he had 100,000,000 bushels as against 95,000,000 bushels at the beginning of the month. It is because of these activities that supporters of the pool claims believe that some payment should be made and that the proper amount is sixty cents per bushel.
The government of the day has come to the conclusion that they are right. We are inclined to believe that they should have that payment in full. This will amount to
86,509,000	with an additional 8350,000 required for the pools that were operating in the coarse grains. We intend to ask them to accept this as final settlement in connection with taking over the wheat and the wheat contracts and the other operations of Mr. McFarland and the government of the day in connection with coarse grains. In conclusion, that is why I move the second reading of the bill which has for its objective the doing of this very thing.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for two hours and a half the chamber has listened to the most violent political speech that I have heard in it for many years about a matter that affects the welfare of every province in the Dominion of Canada, and which was made purely as a vindictive pronouncement against those who had endeavoured to stabilize the price of wheat and prevent disaster from coming to the farmers of western Canada. The hon. gentleman must have realized that he could have said all that is relevant to this measure-I notice the Minister of National Defence is looking up the dictionary; will he look up the word "vindictive"?

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO
speechtext: That is what I am doing.

subtopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO
speechtext:
It is used properly in this instance. I was going to observe that the minister could have dealt with the whole matter on the basis that he has now presented
Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett

it in no more than fifteen minutes. He has presented to the house a bill to which is attached a preamble. There is a rule, which will have to be observed, that you cannot place a preamble in a public bill without offering some public document as proof thereof. I need hardly point out that there is one sentence in the preamble that disposes of this whole matter in its entirety. When I read this to the chamber I am satisfied that every hon. member who knows anything of parliamentary practice and procedure-there are experts among those present -will realize at once that the mere reading of this one paragraph in the preamble would have been sufficient for the purpose of founding this bill. The preamble covers many pages. Let us look at it and see what this particular phase of it is, a rather interesting one too. It asserts that an agreement was made between the wheat board and the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, to take over this wheat. It asserts also that this arrangement was made on December 2, 1935. The following will be found on page 2 of the bill:
Whereas a transfer of wheat and contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat in respect of which the government of Canada had given a guarantee was made by Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, to the Canadian wheat board as of December 2, 1935, subject to final settlement of the terms of such transfer;
There is your connection. There is a settlement of this whole measure made on December 2 and not a single scintilla of evidence has been produced to show what the terms were. The order in council has not been produced. A statement is made in the preamble of a public bill and not a word is given in evidence or a statement made by the minister in charge as to there being any foundation for the statement contained in the bill. I now say that we must have presented to this house-we should have had it when the resolution was before us-the conditions of the contract of December 2, 1935, showing the terms under which this wheat was bought from the wheat pool under Mr. Murray, and bought by him from the wheat producers.
Perhaps the gentleman to whom the minister refers will be able to give us some evidence upon this point. Perhaps the gentleman whose name he was to give us in secret, but not in public, will be able to give us some evidence upon this point. Perhaps the minister himself will be able to give us some evidence upon this point. Perhaps the order in council upon which this bill must be framed will be produced before we proceed

further with this measure, because under the Wheat Board Act enacted last year, section 7, paragraph (f), it was provided that this could be done only with the approval of the governor in council. Where is that approval? Where was it yesterday and the day before when the resolution was under consideration? Where was it during all these discussions that have no relevancy to the matter at all? Why were we not told when the minister stood in his place and imposed-I use the only word that expresses it-a false position upon this committee and upon this house, as to what the facts were, trying to make it appear that this wheat had been purchased by the old board under Mr. McFarland from the wheat producers, whereas he now says, in the bill which we see for the first time to-day, that on the second day of December, 1935, this board acquired this wheat, under terms of which I have no knowledge, under terms of which this house has no knowledge, under terms of which this country has no knowledge, upon which no statement has been made to the press, with respect to which no observations have been made to the people. Nothing of this sort has been done. Why has it not been done? Why have we not been told? That is what I want to know. The house has not forgotten the statement made by the minister that everything was to be done in the open. But is there a man anywhere in this house to-night who can give a statement as to what are the terms of that order in council under which this wheat has been bought? Perhaps the gentleman who gave him his information in secret will now give it to us in public. If we cannot get it from the minister perhaps we will get it from some person on the street corners. It may be published in the Reporter, or what is the name of that journal?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, March 26, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mr. Howe for the second reading of Bill No. 17, respecting the national harbours board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this debate was adjourned I *was endeavouring to urge that in his report Sir Alexander Gibb highly praised the excellence and efficiency of the harbour commissions of Montreal and Vancouver. He said:
They provided a type of administration at least the equal of any that was to be found elsewhere on the north American continent; and notwithstanding mistakes, which no system can prevent, the developments under the two harbour commissions have generally been sound and economically justified.
With regard to costs, at page 73 of the report I find this paragraph:
According to my information, and from the careful inquiries that I have made, I am satisfied that these costs are not seriously challenged by competing ports, except where the latter may be partially assisted by special rail rates.
I also urged that the complete survey and exhaustive investigation had revealed that nowhere in the word is there in existence a system similar to the centralization system provided by this bill. It was tried in France and later discarded as being unsatisfactory and unwarranted; after the laws of 1912 and 1920 autonomous local boards were reverted to.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext: Only in two harbours in France.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
But any other local authority could request the institution of a harbour board. I am referring particularly to the harbours of Le Havre and Bordeaux. I refer again to the Gibb report at page 29, paragraph 75; In the Dutch East Indies a system of departmental officials with local advisory councils, adopted in 1910, has been found to be inflexible, dilatory and unenterprising, and public opinion is veering towards the substitution of practically autonomous local councils or boards. In British India local boards with wide powers are in effect, and the report states that they have obtained considerable success due particularly to the fortunate selection of chairmen and commissioners.
At page 29, paragraph 77 of the report, a parallel is drawn between transportation conditions in India and in Canada, and points of similarity are set out. There seems to be, therefore, some contradictions between the

National Harbours Board-Mr. Vien
findings of fact and the recommendations favouring intense centralization in Canada and also between the suggestion contained at page 31, paragraph S3, that there should be a central board with wide powers, and the recommendation at the same time that considerable latitude should be left to the port manager. If the central board has wide powers, certainly the authority of the port manager must be restricted.
Certain abuses have been pointed out. No doubt they should be corrected, but it seems to me unreasonable and unwise that we should be called upon to scrap a system which has been found to be as excellent and efficient as any to be found elsewhere in order to adopt a system which has been tried in other countries and found unsatisfactory. To my mind the proper remedy is that all capital expenditures should be subject to a vote by parliament; that all expenditures, even of appropriated money, should be subject to approval by order in council, and that all operating receipts and expenditures should be subject to the audit of the auditor general for Canada. Is there anything, for instance, which would prevent the construction of wharves, elevators or other works coming under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works, just as any other public work in Canada does?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member
a question? I should like to inquire whether it is his intention to make a comparison between the section he quoted, paragraph 77 at page 29, and the proposed system embodied in the bill now before the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
I shall leave that to my
hon. friend; I had not contemplated doing that in the remarks I desire to address to the house in the very limited time I have at my disposal. II should like to make clear that the point I am urging the house to consider is that the fullest possible autonomy should be left to the various local port authorities if we want to avoid what has been styled by Sir Alexander Gibb in his report as an inflexible, dilatory and unenterprising system from which public opinion is veering in another country in which that system has been tried.
The conclusions of the report, I am afraid, have been influenced by high officials who in some departments of the state constitute a bureaucracy. I understand their point of view, trying to draw to themselves greater power, influence and emoluments, and no doubt Sir Alexander Gibb had long conferences and consultations with them before he
submitted his report to the government. Such a doctrine of intensified centralization is well known and quite natural in the mouth of our bureaucracy, but to my. mind it is contrary to the spirit and letter of British principles of government and of our own constitutional act. Against that bureaucracy we protested from the stump throughout the country not so very long ago that bureaucracy the immortal Lincoln condemned when he said:
Let us highly resolve that the government of the people, by the people and for the people shall not perish from the earth.
Under British principles of government local autonomy is fostered. These principles did not always obtain; they did not obtain prior to the independence of the United States. But we all know what the results were. They did not obtain in the days which preceded the insurrections of 1837-38 in Canada. We all know what battles were fought to gain responsible government and local jurisdiction and autonomy. Ties freely accepted bind all sections of the British empire. They would become unbearable to any British subject if local autonomy and freedom of action were taken away. British statesmen understood that when self-government was granted to the autonomous dominions. The development and unity of the empire have been maintained only because these principles have been respected.
Sections of our people inhabit distant sections of our country. They differ as to origin, character, traditions and interests. The maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario, the prairie provinces and British Columbia have different problems; they cannot be kept together unless they are allowed to enjoy a fair measure of justice and equity, autonomy and freedom. The rumblings of dissatisfaction, distrust and unrest have often been heard and discussed in this house. I remember the days after 1922 when our Progressive friends from the west in this house threatened secession unless there took place some readjustment of conditions under which they were labouring. They clamoured for the reinstatement of the Crowsnest Pass Agreement Act, and the act was reinstated as far as grain and grain products are concerned. A little later our friends from the maritime provinces also voiced their recriminations against conditions created for them as a result of their entrance into confederation. They said that the natural market for their products was close at hand, but being part of the Dominion of Canada they were excluded from

National Harbours Board-Mr. Vien
the United States market so far as most of their products were concerned. They complained also that they had not received a railway freight rate structure which they had anticipated in their agreement to enter the Canadian confederation. As a result the Duncan report was made and was later implemented by the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
There is at present in Quebec a great body of public opinion holding the view that the
3,000,000 French-Canadians who live in this country do not receive adequate consideration, and the simple reading of the government telephone book bears out the statement that they do not receive fair and equitable treatment in the distribution of government offices. The estimates tabled in this house also show that public moneys are much more freely expended outside Quebec than on matters affecting that province.
People in Quebec, in British Columbia, in the maritime provinces have expressed through their representatives in this house their desire to continue to control their own local affairs. In their opinion the purport of this bill is to withdraw from their hands the administration of their ports, to centralize it in the hands of bureaucratic officials, and so another slice of their local autonomy will have been taken away from them. All this has created in Quebec and elsewhere a great deal of discontent. I should like to read a short article in substantiation of my statement, taken from the Canadian Forum of March, 1936, at page 12, entitled French Canadian Nationalism :
There is a movement on foot amongst the French-Canadians that Canadians would do well to study. Unnoticed by the English press, unsuspected by the public at large, it is steadily gaining strength in Quebec. It has its own clubs, its youth organizations, its newspapers. What is of vastly more importance, it has the backing of the Catholic church.
This is the movement for the creation of an independent French and Catholic republic on the banks of the St. Lawrence.
It is well known that the Abbe Groulx has been preaching this idea for many years. The world war gave it popularity amongst a people conscripted to fight other people's battles on foreign soil, but during the years of "prosperity" little more was heard of it. With the depression, however, it has again sprung into prominence, and this time it is a force to be reckoned with. For Paul Gouin, the leader of the Action Liberale Nationale party, which now holds forty-two seats in the provincial legislature, has himself publicly voiced the hope of French-Canadian independence. Basing himself on the remarks of Cardinal Villeneuve, made in 1922, he recently spoke of the_ "supernatural vocation" of the French race in America, where, in the midst of this north American Babylon it was 
destined to become the "modern Israel." The hope, he admitted, could not be immeditely realized, but it was something towards which his fellow countrymen would never cease to strive.
I am not discussing the merits or demerits of these ideas thus propounded; I am simply urging as a Liberal that the legislation brought down should be revamped to provide the fullest possible measure of autonomy to local authorities, which in my opinion are better able to judge the needs and requirements of the population which they are called upon to serve. I urge that there should be three harbour commissions created, one for the maritime provinces, one for the St. Lawrence river and one for British Columbia; that the best possible men should be selected for these commissions, and that the chairmen of these commissions should be called in an advisory capacity to the minister when needed. Thereby we would retain in each of the different sections of our country local autonomy, and the minister would receive from proper sources the information and assistance of which he stands in need.
I want to conclude by saying that the slogan of all schools of true Liberalism is the utmost possible liberty for every individual and every section of our people. I am not talking of licence; I am speaking of liberty. Any governmental action that interferes with this individual liberty is an attack on liberty itself. The ruggedness, independence, initiative and vigour of the individual are essential factors in the upbuilding of the nation, and they should be encouraged, not stifled, by governmental agencies.
I hope the government will see its way clear to amend its legislation so as to provide these three commissions, one for the maritime provinces, one for the ports on the St. Lawrence river, and one for British Columbia, for thereby it will give to every section of Canada that reasonable degree of local autonomy which we stand for, which they have enjoyed in the past, and which they hold very dear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this bill goes to committee I wish to say just a few words upon it. I do not intend to deal with the merits or the demerits of the bill, but having had a great deal to do with bringing the harbour of Saint John under a commission in 1928, and having heard the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Ryan) deal with this question the other night, I think it is incumbent upon me to draw the attention of the minister to this fact, that the passing of this bill in its present form, repealing as it does the three acts in

National Harbours Board-Mr. Stevens
regard to the harbour of Saint John, I would regard as breaking faith with the port of Saint John if the bill is not amended to protect certain interests in that city.
In the act creating the harbour commission of Saint John there are certain covenants which are not contained in any other harbour commission act, for the reason that Saint John at that date occupied the unique position of being the only harbour in the dominion that had provided its own transportation facilities without any help from the government of Canada in their construction. It is true that the federal government did help through the Department of Public Works in the dredging of the harbour, the dredging of certain places where wharves were constructed, but the real work, the greater part of the construction of those wharves, was carried on and paid for by the city of Saint John itself, at a cost of somewhere between three and four million dollars.
When in 1928 it was decided to place the harbour of Saint John under a commission, the federal government by act of parliament entered into certain agreements with that city. They paid to Saint John a valuation fixed by arbitrators for the constructions which the city had carried on for a number of years. The city passed over to His Majesty the King, not to the harbour commission of Saint John, certain properties, and those properties were to be administered by a harbour commission. There are in that act certain covenants by which the city of Saint John binds itself to do certain things provided the government, on its part, at a later period does certain things. If the bill now before the house is adopted in its present form without amendment, it will be breaking faith with the city or harbour of Saint John, and I would ask the minister seriously to consider an amendment to the bill by which those covenants entered into in 1928 will be properly safeguarded and satisfaction in every way given to the people of the constituency of Saint John-AIbert.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise not to offer any serious criticism of the bill but rather to make a few suggestions which I hope the minister and his colleagues will take into consideration and possibly, as suggested by my hon. friend from one of the Montreal ridings, amend the bill before it is finally disposed of by this house.
Perhaps it might not be out of place for me to say a few words regarding the origin of the organization of the great port of Vancouver and the creation of a harbour commission there. It was one of the first tasks I undertook when I entered parliament
twenty-five years ago. My proposal at that time to the government of the day, the Minister of Marine then being, I think, the Hon. Mr. Hazen, later Sir Douglas Hazen, was a form of commission similar to the Mersey Trust of Liverpool or the Port Trust of London. I believe that a similar type of port administration is in vogue in Sydney, and of course in other ports. I made a very careful study at the time of the Mersey Trust of Liverpool and of the London Port Trust. The principle involved there is that responsible groups such as shippers, handlers of cargoes, shipping interests, the board of trade and bodies of that kind, and the city itself, I believe, have the nominating of the members of what is known as the Port Trust. I am not familiar with what may have been done in recent years to amend that organization, but I know that in those days it was along the lines I have mentioned, and so I had prepared a bill, and proposed it to the government of the day, for setting up such an organization for the harbour of Vancouver. Furthermore, it was proposed in that bill that such bodies should control not only the harbour of Burrard inlet, or Vancouver itself, but also the mouth of the Fraser river and New Westminster. Later on two other harbour commissions were created, one at New Westminster, and another one known as the North Fraser harbour board, which, I believe, was later merged with the Vancouver harbour board.
I think any student of the situation on the Pacific coast will admit that it would be in the interest of the public generally if there was some authority directly over all these activities in the lower mainland. In any case I would suggest to the minister that before this bill is finally passed consideration should be given to some form of local council, an advisory council, if you will, which, I believe, has already been suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). There should be some form of local advisory council to act in cooperation with the board proposed to be set up under this bill.
That is one suggestion, but I was also impressed the other day by the observations of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). Lie referred to the matter of harbour boundaries and expressed some doubt as to the adequacy of this bill in preserving the present boundaries of harbours or in giving legal status to them. Coming from one of his experience and standing as a lawyer, that, I admit, rather perturbed
1560	COMMONS
National Harbours Board-Mr. Stevens
me, because on looking over the bill I notice that in reference to boundaries it simply declares in subsection 2 of section 6 that:
The boundaries of the harbours of Halifax, Saint John, Chicoutimi, Quebec, Three Rivers, Montreal and Vancouver shall be as described in the several acts constituting the corporations, or as may be determined from time to time by order of the governor in council, and any such order shall be published in the Canada Gazette.
Then I notice that at the conclusion of the bill there is this section, 39:
The acts mentioned in the schedule to this act and the Quebec Harbour and River Police Act, chapter one hundred and sixty-nine of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, are hereby repealed.
I see, in connection with this very lengthy schedule, there are several acts relating to the harbour of Vancouver, including the original act of incorporation, which are all repealed.
I am not a lawyer, nor do I ever dare to offer views on law, but following the expressions of doubt by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George I am going to ask the minister to have this point very carefully checked, whether in view of the repeal of the other acts, the original act and its amending acts, this description in the present bill is sufficient to preserve the legality of the boundaries of Vancouver harbour. I do not speak without some knowledge. As I say, I do not pretend to express my legal views; far be it from me to dare to do that in this house, but I do speak from some knowledge of the difficulties that have arisen from time to time. For instance, I would remind the government-and if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) were in his seat he would recall it at once, because he was an arbitrator in the matter-of the dispute between the harbour commission of Vancouver, acting under the dominion government, and the provincial authorities regarding the boundaries of Vancouver harbour in False Creek, and also the dispute as to the right or the jurisdiction of the harbour commissioners in extending out along Point Grey, although I find that in the act constituting the original charter of Vancouver harbour it describes the harbour as all within Point Atkinson and Point Grey. But I am quite certain that at the present time, or for some time since this dispute with the provincial government, the harbour commissioners have not actually had jurisdiction.
The minister must bear in mind that merely stating in this measure that the boundaries shall be as described in the various acts incorporating these harbours, will scarcely

protect the new form of administration in their control over the territory which supposedly is now within the harbour. I think there is a real difficulty there and one which should be very carefully considered. It is not something to be treated lightly, because it affects, for instance, the question of ships moving within the area, the control of the foreshore, the right to construct wharves, or the right of the administration to indicate the kind of docks that shall be constructed. So many factors, so many activities are affected, that nothing but grief can come unless there is great safeguard provided in the bill. That is the second point I would bring to the attention of the minister.
The third point I suggest is this: While I have not fully considered the question of bylaws, I should like to ask the minister when we get into the committee stage to be prepared to demonstrate that the power under the new measure covers fully the powers in the present individual harbour commissioners' acts with respect to bylaws. I am a little doubtful whether certain powers are taken in this new legislation which are at present in existence, having been found to be very necessary. Let me refer, for example, to matters of order and regularity and the prevention of theft and depredation. The harbour commissioners of Vancouver- and I speak only for them-have worked out a system of cooperation with the city police. Whether it is still in existence I am not certain, but I know that for a great many years it worked very satisfactorily, and I regard it aS of considerable importance, because after all the line of demarcation between the property of the harbour commissioners and that which is directly under the city is undoubtedly difficult to define or to keep track of. My hon. friend from Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), who is the mayor of the city, will be in a better position to speak on that point than I am.
There is another very important matter and I admit it is highly controversial so far as Vancouver is concerned. There is a great difference of opinion regarding it among the authorities, and while I respect the opinion of others who differ from myself on it, yet I think it is a matter that is of first importance. I refer to the question of harbour railway control or, as the powers of bylaw in the old act recite, the regulation of railway and other traffic on the quays and wharves of the corporation in the harbour, the prevention and removal of obstructions, impediments or hindrances to traffic, and furthermore the enforcement of arrangements made or to be made under the powers given

National Harbours Board-Mr. Stevens
by the act with railway companies having connection with the harbour.
I would impress upon the minister the fact that there are some very sharp cleavages of opinion with respect to the interpretation of the rights of the Canadian Pacific railway and of the Canadian National Railways in Vancouver. I am not putting that in quite proper language, because it is necessary to understand the situation physically in order to interpret what I am saying. The Canadian Pacific railway has an excellent position in regard to the waterfront of the harbour of Vancouver; on the other hand the Canadian National has but very meagre access to the waterfront of the main harbour of that city. The Canadian National comes from Westminster over the Great Northern railway, so far as passenger traffic is concerned, and freight traffic as well is switched across from there. Its access to the harbour is certainly very much restricted at the present time. Shortly after the incorporation of Vancouver harbour I made a personal study of the situation. I urged upon the government, of the day, and did so for years and yeaTs, the establishment of a terminal harbour railway. The story is quite a long one.
I frankly admit that there were those of eminent authority, whose views merited every consideration, who took the attitude that this should not be done; that the Canadian Pacific railway could handle all the traffic to the wharves. I do not wish to say anything derogatory of the Canadian Pacific railway, but I think it would be asking perhaps too much of human nature to expect the officials of one great railway company to treat with impartiality traffic originating from or to go over the rails of another competing system. I do not think that is possible of attainment. In saying this I want to make it very clear that I am not reflecting upon the excellent character of the chief officials of the Canadian Pacific railway in Vancouver. Indeed, I think I can count most of them as my friends. However I think it is asking more than human nature is capable of discharging to expect that they would allow traffic to go off their lines on to another line with absolute impartiality. If a shipper desired that this should be done, of course it would be done, as we all know the law, but we are all aware that many little impediments could be thrown in the way of the movement of goods from one line on to another.
All through the years I felt that it was highly desirable that a harbour terminal railway should be established in Vancouver, and
it was so established. This railway has not made the progress I hoped it would although it has been developed to a certain extent. I think there are a couple of locomotives owned by the harbour commission which move cars into the government wharves and elevators or take cars from the Canadian National and the Great Northern rails to the wharves or for interchange with the Canadian Pacific, or vice versa. I believe this ought to be developed more completely, and may I say to the minister that that administration under the old commission is not carried into force in this new bill.
I am going to say very frankly what is in my mind. What I am afraid of is that in the drafting of this bill this matter has been overlooked, and when it becomes law we shall wake up to the fact that the Canadian Pacific railway controls absolutely the movement of freight in the harbour of Vancouver. I want to place myself clearly on record so that we shall not be surprised and taken unawares later on should this happen. Again, 1 repeat that in making this statement I am in no sense reflecting on the management of the Canadian Pacific railway. I assert that we ought not to subject the Canadian National, the Great Northern, the Northern Pacific or the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul or other railways having access to Vancouver from the south or over the Canadian National lines to the control of the Canadian Pacific in that way. I think that is all I wish to say in connection with the bylaws. I submit to the minister before I leave this point that I do not think the new bill makes provision for taking care of this situation to which I have referred.
There is one other point I wish to make. It must be borne in mind that Vancouver is in competition directly and most acutely with the port of Seattle, and to a lesser degree with the ports of Portland, Tacoma and San Francisco. That may not mean much to one who is unacquainted with traffic on the Pacific, but when one considers that competition in trade moving from the American continent to the orient is largely a matter of the route over which the traffic moves, thep he gets some idea of the importance of the control of the harbour at Vancouver or Prince Rupert or the other ports. However, it must be recognized that Vancouver is the port through which the great movement of goods occurs. Unless there is full provision for meeting that competition this bill will be a retrograde movement. I strongly advise the creation of a local advisory council, or the government could make me extremely happy by organizing

National Harbours Board-Mr. Stevens
something along the lines of the Mersey Trust to which I have already referred. If we do not anticipate meeting this competition, we may lose this trade in such a way as never to recover it.
I am somewhat handicapped in not having any records before me, but I should like to indicate the nature of this competition. For instance, it occurs in the facilities of berthing, the regulations controlling the movement of ships in the harbour. Another form of competition is in connection with rates on a great variety of cargo. Rates on grain are not so significant, but rates on canned salmon and upon other special classes of cargo moving in and out of these ports are important. I will give an illustration. Prior to a very few years ago there were no facilities in the port of Vancouver for handling vegetable oils. That may not seem an important matter to those who think a few tons of vegetable oil will not make much difference, but it might mean that a ship would go to Seattle instead of coming into Vancouver. Frequently a steamer with a full cargo has been sent to Seattle to unload because there were no facilities in Vancouver to take care of vegetable oils. Seattle thus got the advantage not only of handling oils but of handling all the other cargoes. Facilities were created in the harbour of Vancouver to handle these oils, which assisted in the movement of goods.
Another line of competition is in pilotage charges, but that is not a matter for the harbour commissioners. There are also port charges of various kinds. Then, there is the question of silk shipments which enters quite another field. The shipment of silk depends largely upon dispatch, but I am sorry to say that this traffic has dropped off materially in recent years because the silk is now carried from Japan and the orient through the Panama canal to New York and other ports on the Atlantic. On the other hand, it has been one of the most valuable items of traffic through Canada ever since I went to British Columbia forty-two years ago. I can remember when the old Empress liners of the Canadian Pacific, little 5,000 ton boats, used to bring in cargoes of silk. Special trains would be waiting which would have the right of way over the fastest passenger trains to carry the silk across the continent for shipment to Great Britain. Down through the years the competition for this silk has been extremely keen; the Canadian Pacific are operating some very fine vessels on the Pacific, and we should take more care in guarding the facilities of the harbour in that respect.
I am not going to delay the house with a further argument on the matter. I trust
[Mr. Stevens. 1
the minister will not think I am opposing in any sense his efforts to improve the administration of the harbours of Canada. In that respect I am entirely in sympathy with him. At the same time I recognize that there have been weaknesses in connection with the harbours.
I cannot speak as to the last two years, but prior to two years ago the harbour of Vancouver had paid in full its interest on loans from the government and had maintained its sinking fund intact. I am not quite certain whether that has been continued right up to the present; I think not; but on the whole it will be found that it has paid its interest and maintained its sinking fund in pretty good shape, the interest rate, which I think used to be 5^ per cent, being reduced to five per cent. I suggest, if this matter is not covered in the new bill, that the interest rate should be reduced materially, because five per cent is too high a rate for a public body of that kind to be asked to maintain under modern conditions.
Again I say that I do not wish to leave the impression that I am criticizing the minister for his bill. I think the tone of the debate, and particularly the observations of my hon. friends the member for Outremont ('Mr. Vien), the member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), and the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), have been such that the minister will agree they have been full of constructive suggestions and have displayed a genuine anxiety to do what is in the best interests of the country. In that spirit I offer these few suggestions to the minister.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
There is one matter to which I should like to direct attention because it is fundamental to port development in Canada. I associate myself with the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Vien) and the hon. member for East Kootenay (Mr. Stevens), and base what I have to say very largely upon Sir Alexander Gibb's findings as set out in section 83 of the report. He says:
It is essential to avoid emasculating the local administration, since no centralized control can replace an efficient and active local administration, or the special knowledge and initiative of the local business community, both of which are vital to a port's prosperity.
I unhesitatingly condemn, on conclusions sanctioned by past experience, the centralization in the city of Ottawa of the control of the development of the port of Vancouver. I have no reason to believe that men living in Ottawa can ever have the understanding, the sympathy and the faith that are neces-

National Harbours Board-Mr. McGeer
sary to support and sustain the development of a port upon the Pacific ocean. The government of Canada, unfortunately, I think, for the dominion, is to some extent in an out-of-the-way place. I think a majority of members overlook the fact that there is such a thing as the Atlantic ocean; and that being so, it is hardly reasonable to expect them to appreciate that there is such a thing as the Pacific ocean. I remember one day appearing before the board of railway commissioners, and I wanted to emphasize the fact; I said, "Mr. Chairman, I would like to put something on record this morning." He said, "Very well, what is it?" I said, "Mr. Chairman, I would like to record that Vancouver is in Canada, on this side of the Pacific ocean, and incidentally, on this side of Tokyo, Japan." The chairman of the board of railway commissioners said, "I think, Mr. McGeer, everybody on the board is aware of that fact." I said, "Mr. Chairman, when I looked at the rates on grain moving from Calgary to Vancouver and checked then* up with the rates on grain from Calgary to Tokyo, I found that it costs considerably more to move grain from Calgary to Vancouver than it does to Tokyo, and I therefore suspected that somebody might have misplaced the location of Vancouver and Tokyo."
Let me draw to the attention of the house one other illustration of what Sir Alexander Gibb had in mind when he referred to initiative of a type that grows out of the business community around the port as being essential to the port's well-being. In 1914 the Panama canal was completed. That great achievement of the United States republic synchronized with another great achievement of the north American continent, the completion of the Canadian National or the Canadian Northern Pacific railway through the Yellowhead pass, which meant a complete elimination of mountain grades on Canada's internal transportation systems as far as the Rocky and the Selkirk mountains were concerned. Everyone believed that as a result of the completion of the railway through the Yellowhead pass and the completion of the Panama canal, Vancouver would become a world port distributing grain from western Canada to the advantage of the Alberta farmer.
