speechtext: And it did.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext: My friend says that it did, and very largely through his intelligent efforts, for which we in the west are profoundly thankful.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext: Thank you.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF PUBLIC HARBOURS
speechtext:
But not until men of the superior intelligence of the hon. member for Outremont graced the board of railway commissioners. "Yes, it did/' says my hon. friend, but the hon. member for East Kootenay remembers the construction of the elevator and its completion in 1916, and its standing idle on the shore of Burrard inlet until many years afterwards, when rate adjustments were made and general prejudices were broken down. Once the board of railway commissioners reduced the rate on grain to the port of Vancouver to a basis, not of equality but of a reduction of the discrimination to a measurable equality, Vancouver became the greatest grain port in the world, and is in that happy position to-day. I quite appreciate the fact that that never would have happened had it been left to men in Ottawa, subject to the influence of everything from Winnipeg to the Atlantic seaboard, including not only the port of Buffalo, but the port of the city of New York. I cannot quite understand how this particular commission can function in Vancouver and have a harbour commission functioning in New Westminster.
The point mentioned by the hon. member for East Kootenay is of the utmost importance. To-day the port of Vancouver serves a great many railways, the British Columbia Electric, the Great Northern, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, but I wonder whether hon. members are aware of the fact that the Canadian National system ends at Port Mann on the banks of the Eraser river and can come into the port of Vancouver only over a leased foreign railway under circumstances which make the cost of moving freight from Port Mann into the shipping basin of Burrard inlet, which is under the jurisdiction of the Vancouver harbour commissioners, almost as great as the cost of moving freight from Alberta to Port Mann. The necessity of the harbour development of Vancouver is the very thing that Sir Alexander Gibb pointed out as being essential, and that is ignored and overlooked in this bill.
I want to appeal to the minister to reconsider that particular phase of the matter, because I must say this: After all, we hope that Canada can continue to be a united nation from the Atlantic to the Pacific, but I want to say to the members of this government that when you assume the responsibility for centralizing control of port development at Ottawa you also assume responsibility for avoiding sectional dissatisfaction with administration in Ottawa, and there are a great many who are beginning to feel that there is not the consideration coming from the central authority in Ottawa that makes it to the best

1564	COMMONS
National Harbours Board-Mr. Howe
interests of sections at far distant points to remain in confederation. It is all very well to say that we are going to improve the administration of the harbours of Halifax and Vancouver, but let me point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that Vancouver is competing with Seattle in one of the world's most rapidly developing and most important shipping basins, namely the gulf of Georgia and Puget sound. If one takes a trip along the Pacific coast, as I did recently, and notes what is taking place in San Diego, San Pedro, San Francisco bay and Seattle, it will be recognized that Vancouver is now moving into competition with ports on the Pacific coast that have the backing of the United States government, which is establishing a naval war strength on the Pacific surpassing anything ever developed by any other nation in the world. So, it is not going to be easy to maintain the standard of port service in Vancouver without very much in the way of faith in the future as to what the Pacific ocean trade will be, and if a federal control assumes the responsibility, that responsibility must be fulfilled to a much greater extent than anything that has been undertaken in the past.
There is one other section of the bill to which I should like to refer; that is the section with reference to the power to make rates. Section 15 of the bill reads:
The board may levy such rates and tolls as are fixed by bylaw and may, with the approval of the minister, commute any rates-
I quite appreciate that in the administration jf a port like Vancouver, which competes not only with the other Pacific coast ports but with ports throughout the world, bargaining for traffic is essential, but I question the wisdom of having the power to commute rates left to the responsibility of a minister of the crown. In the first place such power vested in a minister is a power that the minister will hesitate to exercise for fear of partisan criticism. That will mean delays, deferred action and lack of action which will work against the best interests of the port.
I only want to say that nothing is more important in the life of the Dominion of Canada to-day than the development of our internal and external transportation systems, and nothing can make a greater contribution to economic recovery than the proper and effective development of our Canadian port facilities, for we are just as much a maritime nation as is Great Britain. For the distribution of our products into the markets of the world we are not going to find our facilities

completed by the development of internal systems; we must go forward on a much wider basis than has been the case previously in the development of our ports and our external facilities for the distribution of our goods.
I reserve my further remarks until we are in committee on this bill, but I should like to close with this appeal to the government and to the minister in charge of this bill. In your desire to provide efficient and economic administration do not overlook the fact that there is something to be gleaned and something to be gained by respecting the autonomy and the power of loyal communities to build up their own trading facilities.

Mr. Speaker, I had intended to make some rather extended remarks in closing this debate, but as the hour is getting late and I should like to have a vote before eleven o'clock I shall be very brief. I want to say that I appreciate the friendly and helpful spirit in which this debate has been conducted. A great many suggestions have been made; every one of them has been and is being analyzed by the officers of my department, and each will be discussed when the bill is in committee. I may say that the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Ryan) brought to my attention one omission which was made. I do not know that the omission would have meant anything very serious, because of course we would have respected the spirit of it, but we did omit an essential portion, and an amendment has been prepared restoring that to the bill. Similarly other suggestions, on being examined, have been found to have merit, and there again amendments are being prepared.
The suggestion has been made that this bill has been hastily drawn up. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it has been a most laborious task to prepare the bill, and it has been in the course of preparation for some three months. I am not a legal man, but I have been in a number of conferences attempting to guide the spirit and tone of the thing. We have had the best legal assistance obtainable in the public service, from the officers of the Department of Justice and the legal officers of the Department of Railways. The bill has been carefully studied, but it is a very large subject and it is obvious that further suggestions have to be made. I dare say that after we have finished with it in the committee we shall find that in practice further improvements can still be made. One

Questions
point I have noticed with great interest is how many copies of the Gibb report are in circulation. I thought they would all have been lost in the four years since the report was brought down, but they are all out and dusted off and we have heard a good deal about it. Once again let me thank hon. members on both sides of the house for the helpful spirit in which they have examined this bill. Any further remarks I will reserve until the committee stage.

I wish to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) a question. It was announced some time ago by the United States treasury that the United States was purchasing silver from the Bank of Canada. If that is true, is the United States government making payment 
in silver certificates or in federal reserve notes, which are not legal tender in Canada, or in gold, for the silver purchased from the Bank of Canada?
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): The agents for the United States treasury in the purchase of silver are the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The Bank of Canada, in selling silver to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, acting on behalf of the United States treasury, receives payment by way of credit to the account of the Bank of Canada in the Federal Reserve Bank of New York in United States funds. As the purchaser of silver the United States pays in its own funds. If Canadian funds are required the Bank of Canada of course sells United States funds at the current rate of exchange and purchases Canadian funds.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE

speechtext:
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 14, respecting the establishment of a national employment commission.
He said:	In moving the second reading
of this bill I am fully aware of my responsibility as a member of the government in commending this legislation to the favourable consideration of the house. The problem of prolonged unemployment in this and other countries is a challenge to the political intelligence of our generation. No one can have a daily contact with that problem without realizing that upon our ability to deal with it effectively may depend the maintenance of institutions and traditions which have long been established in this country. I have no desire to exaggerate the gravity of the situation. As a matter of fact I shall point out presently that we have strong grounds for confidence as we face the immediate future. Nevertheless, even when it is conceded that there has been a perceptible improvement in economic conditions during the past year, we are still faced with the fact that the problem of unemployment remains unsolved. Moreover the resources of public finance have been impaired in the interval as a result of mounting debts and increasing taxes which have been incurred and imposed as internal measures of defence against want and destitution. This much may be said at
the outset in order to emphasize the importance of the question which is now before us for consideration.
I do not suggest that any member of this house is wanting in a sense of obligation to find a remedy for unemployment. It is well to remember, however, that familiarity sometimes breeds indifference, and our constant companionship with unemployment and relief these past few years may lead us to accept it as a disagreeable but inevitable feature of our social environment in the post-war world. As individuals we must guard ourselves against the complacent acceptance of conditions as we find them to-day. As members of parliament and as a government the placid acceptance of present conditions would be little better than a voluntary declaration of political bankruptcy.
There is another consideration which no one will wish to overlook at this time. Our experience of unemployment has brought home to us more forcibly than any other feature of government policy that it is the constant purpose of the state to promote the welfare of its members and that the organized power of the state should be used steadfastly towards a realization of that purpose. During the past few years Canada and other countries have suffered incalculable injury as a result of the dislocation of international trade and a very serious contraction of normal industrial activity. The victims of the depression in Canada alone may be counted by the hundred thousand. We often think and speak of this problem in statistical terms; we are compelled to do so for purposes of comparison and analysis; but behind these figures of unemployment and relief there is, as each of us well knows, the harsh reality of human privation and frustration. Even when we deal with it objectively, as we are compelled to do, we must be conscious at all times of the extraordinary patience and fortitude of those whose lot it has been to go in company with fear and pain during a period which now exceeds the duration of the world war. We could ask no higher incentive for our labours here than the remembrance of the manner in which our people generally have endured the conditions which have prevailed during these troubled and trying years.
The major proposal contained in this bill is not new. It was urged most strongly upon the late administration by the present Prime Minister in succeeding sessions of the last parliament. On every such occasion the proposal was rejected, and for reasons which, I venture to say, carried less conviction with each passing year. The final decision, however, lay with the government of the day, and that government made it
1570	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Rogers
abundantly clear that it did not recognize the necessity or the advantage of establishing a representative national body to assist in the formulation of measures to deal with unemployment and relief. It may be conceded that there is room for honest difference of opinion as to the utility of a national commission of this kind to assist the state in a period of grave economic crisis. The late administration held one view on this matter; we hold the contrary view. In the general elections of last October the issue between us was referred to the electorate. It is needless to point out that policies in relation to unemployment and relief occupied a very prominent place among the various questions that were pronounced upon by the Canadian people at that time. As a result of the verdict of the electorate, we are now under a new dispensation, and this government is pledged to approach the urgent problem of unemployment upon the basis of a nation wide cooperative effort through the medium of a national employment commission. The measure now before the house is evidence of our intention to carry out this undertaking.
On second reading of a bill, Mr. Speaker, it is the practice to confine debate to the principle of the proposed legislation-

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
-leaving the details for discussion in the committee stage. The principle of this bill may be expressed very briefly. We have to determine whether the abnormal conditions created by unemployment and relief require something more than the normal machinery of government to deal with them effectively. If wre are agreed that the normal machinery of government is inadequate to meet the existing situation we must then consider whether a national employment commission as provided in this bill will perform a useful function as an aid to government in attacking this stubborn problem that has defied solution during the past five years.
May I say at once that we as a government have faced these questions and have answered them in the affirmative, and I hope it may be possible to persuade the house generally that in making this decision and in bringing down this legislation we are taking appropriate measures for an organized effort to meet the most serious challenge that has confronted this country in a time of peace.
In supporting the proposals set out in this bill, Mr. Speaker, I wish to state and discuss some of the broad considerations of policy which call for the establishment of a national employment commission at this time. May I first state these considerations and then develop them in the order given:

1.	After an experience of five years we are compelled to recognize that unemployment is a persistent condition which does not respond quickly to ordinary legislative methods. This suggests the wisdom of a national survey of the entire problem as a preliminary to the formulation of long range measures to expand employment and thereby reduce the tax burden of relief.
2.	Previous administrative methods have failed to secure and utilize information respecting unemployment and relief which would make it possible to subdivide the problem into its various sections of economic and social significance.
3.	In our federal constitution there is a well established division of responsibility in relation both to the administration of relief and to the maintenance of social services. In order to avoid friction or duplication in the administration of relief it is necessary to secure a more effective and continuous coordination of effort in relation to the entire problem. Experience has proved the need of some kind of nexus, or connecting link, between the various governmental agencies having a responsibility in relation to relief.
4.	The experience of the past five years has also proved beyond question that it is not within the power of government to end unemployment by its own unaided efforts. There is a growing recognition that victory over the depression and unemployment cannot be won by a pitched battle on any front, but only by a sustained campaign along the entire front of our economic life. The success of this campaign requires that the leadership of government should be supported and supplemented by the cooperative effort of organized industry and commerce, financial institutions, labour organizations and social service agencies throughout the entire dominion.
Those, sir, are the broad considerations of public policy upon which we believe it is possible and desirable to erect at this time a national employment commission as a means of affording advice and also of securing the coordination of all governmental agencies in a determined effort to deal constructively, and I trust successfully, with this problem of unemployment.
Let me refer now to the persistence and the magnitude of the problem of unemployment and relief as it exists to-day and as it has developed during the past five years. Members of the house may recall that in a previous debate I gave an undertaking that on second reading of this bill I would place

I should like now to deal with the employment situation as it is revealed in the figures supplied by the bureau of statistics, and also to give a synopsis of the figures of relief recipients which I have just presented to the house. There are two statistical indices showing the trend of employment and industry throughout Canada, both of which are now available over a considerable period of years. One is the series of index numbers of employment in industries other than farming, fishing and domestic service, compiled by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics from reports furnished by employers; the other is the series giving the percentages

of their members who are unemployed as reported by the trade unions to the Department of Labour.
Let us consider first the index numbers of employment, and what conclusions we are justified in drawing at this time from a study of those index numbers. The bureau of statistics index numbers are all related to a base of 100 points which represents the average for the months of the year 1926. In other words the average figures of employment for 1926 are taken as the base. The index for March 1, 1936, stood at 98-9. The pre-depression peak for the same month, March, was reached in 1929 when the figure

Employment Commission-Mr. Rogers
was 111-4. March, 1930, showed only a slight decline, to 110-2. The index therefore shows a net drop on March 1 of this year compared with the same date in 1930 of approximately 10-2 per cent.
But this does not mean that the drop in employment in the six years has been only 10-2 per cent; for otheT factors enter. Those factors arise chiefly from two considerations. First, these index numbers do not take into account the normal increase in population. Assuming the percentage of the population seeking gainful employment remains constant, then the number seeking gainful employment increases each year in proportion to the gain in general population. The estimate of population increase over 1930 is approximately eight per cent, so that this factor would indicate the need of adding a minimum of eight per cent to the visible difference between March of 1930 and March of 1936 to measure more nearly the net decrease in employment in that period. The reason for referring to this addition as a minimum is that not all persons were employed on March 1, 1930. If such addition be made it would indicate a net relative decrease of at least 18-2 per cent in the employment reported upon in the six years up to March 1, 1936.
A little later I propose to refer to a feature of our economic situation which in our consideration of the problem in the past few years has, I believe, been overlooked. I refer to seasonal unemployment This country is susceptible in a peculiar degree to seasonal variations of employment. Referring again to the index numbers may I explain that there are included as employed persons some thousands who are on relief works or are in relief camps. The figure for March 1, 1936, is thus supported by this factor, while that for March 1, 1930, was not influenced in like manner. In the nature of things it is proper that we speak of these men on relief works as employed persons. At the same time in our consideration of the implication of these figures it is rather important that we make the necessary deductions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

municipalities, provinces and the dominion?

speechtext:
Yes, engaged on relief
works generally. It is to be noted that the index numbers relate to industrial employment only. Among other industries they exclude farming. Due to crop conditions in recent years the farming industry is now able to absorb substantially fewer men than it did in normal times. This factor is not covered in the index numbers, and figures are lacking on this phase of employment. However,
observations lead to the belief that the decrease in farm employment afforded would be at least as great as that in industrial employment. I hope it will be possible presently to obtain further and more accurate information upon this phase of the problem. Thus to indicate the probable decline of 18-2 per cent in general employment from March 1, 1930, to March 1, 1936, is not to overlook the fact that the same index numbers show that material progress has been made in the recovery of employment since the low of the depression. That low was reached on April 1, 1933; but to use the same month as we used before, March, at which time the index stood at 76-9-a very low point indeed in relation to the basal figure of 100, which represents the average of employment in the year 1926. From March 1, 1933, to March 1, 1936, the index moved up 22 points, or approximately 28-6 per cent. I believe we are justified in saying that there is some cause for encouragement in that improvement. This 28-6 per cent improvement upon the low point of March 1, 1933, may be taken to indicate the extent of employment recovery in the last three years, subject to a deduction of at least four per cent for the assumed increase in the numbers of persons seeking gainful work.
To sum up, Dominion Bureau of Statistics index numbers of employment in industries other than farming, fishing and domestic services, indicate that at March 1 of this year industrial employment showed an apparent net recovery of not more than 24-6 per cent in relation to March 1, 1933, which was the low point, but a net decrease of not less than 18-2 per cent relative to March 1, 1930. These are the figures after making allowances to compensate for the normal growth in the number of persons seeking gainful employment. In these calculations allowances not made, however, are those for the influence of relief work on the trend of employment. It should also be pointed out that these percentages are not directly comparable one to the other, as they are on different bases, that of the recovery being based on the abnormally low level of 1933.

speechtext: Has the hon. member the actual figures?

speechtext:
I am sorry I have not the figures with me. If I can obtain them I shall be very pleased to do so during the committee stage.
May I add a word in parenthesis at this time to the effect that it is extremely difficult to get an actual computation of the employment created by relief works. For example,
1574	COMMONS
Employment Commission-Mr. Rogers
on highways immediate employment is afforded to those doing actual construction work, but it has always been the hope of governments in connection with any program of public works that there would be collateral employment created, and that the industries which provide materials used on highways, as a result of such expenditures would be able to expand employment. Indeed I believe it is that criterion which to a great extent ought to guide us in determining the direction of our expenditures on relief works.
I now come to the figures on employment as revealed by the trade unions. The general trend of employment, as shown by the index numbers, is corroborated in a general way by the Department of Labour figures of unemployment. The recession in employment set in somewhat earlier among trade unions than was indicated by the index numbers of general employment. On February 28, 1930 the percentage of unemployment was 11-5 per cent. For the same date, the last day of February in succeeding years, the heaviest unemployment was reported on February 28, 1933, when it was 24-3 per cent. I might say that when we take the February figures we do bring in prominently the feature of seasonal unemployment in the construction industries. On February 29 of this year there was a net reduction shown in unemployment in the trade unions, the figure standing at 13-8 per cent. So that in the figures supplied by the trade unions we do find corroboration of the conclusions which would reasonably be based upon a study of the index numbers of employment established by the bureau of statistics.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I take it that included all trade unions.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
All unions reporting to the Department of Labour, and my impression is that that is nearly all-inclusive. Again if I find my statement is not correct I shall be pleased to make the necessary correction in committee. In neither of these two indices is any allowance made for persons in part time employment. I refer to persons working less than the normal working week, of whom there were a considerable number at all times during the depression. So much, then, for the employment situation as it exists to-day.
It does seem to me that the analysis of the situation based upon these figures points very clearly to the magnitude of the problem stiil confronting us, and to the persistence of the unemployment situation.
I now come to the second consideration of policy which in our view recommends the establishment at this time of a national em-

ployment commission. Hon. members will recall that the first consideration was the persistent magnitude of the problem. I believe that factor has been demonstrated beyond any possibility of contradiction. The next point was that previous administrative methods failed to secure and utilize information respecting unemployment and relief which would make it possible to subdivide the problem into its various sections of economic and social significance. Hon. members may recall that during a previous discussion I made the statement that when I became Minister of Labour, the Department of Labour did not have in its possession and had not been previously instructed to obtain that information respecting the unemployment and relief situation which would have made it possible for us to analyze and interpret the relief problem in terms of human values. I think some exception was taken at that time to my use of the term "human values," but I made it quite clear that I had in view that information respecting the situation which would enable us to examine it in its true economic and social significance, including the collection of information respecting the previous occupations of those who were unemployed and the length of time recipients of relief had been receiving state assistance.
At the dominion-provincial conference held in December of last year a subconference on unemployment and relief considered the data which were available in respect of relief recipients, particularly as to its adequacy as a basis for a comprehensive study of the relief situation. Finding that it was desirable to have statistics much more complete as a regular feature of relief administration, a subcommittee was appointed to inquire into this question under the chairmanship of Doctor R. H. Coats, dominion statistician. This subcommittee, which consisted of representatives of the dominion and the several provinces, recommended that a reregistration of direct relief recipients be undertaken by the provinces and the municipalities for the purpose of procuring uniform data. It was suggested that the provinces would forward to the Department of Labour the data secured in order that a tabulation and analysis might be made, thus ensuring a classification of direct relief recipients on a dominion basis. A technique, including specimen forms, was also recommended. This report of the subcommittee was adopted by the subconference on unemployment and relief. In giving consideration to the establishment of a national employment commission, the subconference considered the recommendation in connection

Employment Commission-Mr. Rogers
with statistics embodied in the subcommit' tee's report and proposed the following:
In cooperation with the provinces and municipalities to carry out as early as possible a dominion-wide registration and classification of those on relief who are capable of selfsupporting work.
After further consideration following the conference it was the opinion of the Department of Labour that the collection of statistics adequate to warrant a classification of persons on relief would involve some considerable time, so much so that if statistics were to be available within a reasonable time after the establishment of the proposed commission it would be desirable that steps should be taken forthwith to put into effect a new statistical system in order that later delays might be obviated. With this object in view various forms were drafted by the Department of Labour and were distributed about the middle of January, to be returned in their completed form each month by the provinces and municipalities to the department at Ottawa. At this point I should like to say that in connection with this effort to obtain more adequate information we have received nothing but the most cordial cooperation from the provinces and municipalities concerned. I take it that this is due to their realization of the value, certainly at this stage of the problem, of this more precise information which will enable us to divide this problem of unemployment and relief into its appropriate sections of social and economic significance. If we simply consider the numbers of those who are on relief, running over a million, the problem seems staggering and discouraging and almost insoluble. A great Greek philosopher, with whom I am sure my right hon. friend is familiar, once said that if we desire to solve a complex problem we should resolve it into its elements. That is what I believe we can do in connection with this whole question of the classification of those on relief. I believe it is going to assist us to approach in a more scientific and I trust more sensible way the whole matter. To what extent actual reregistration of those on relief should be undertaken in order to accommodate the records of the municipalities to the statistical requirements of the Department of Labour was left to the provinces and the municipalities to determine, each for themselves, more particularly in view of the fact that several of the larger municipalities had then but recently completed such reregistration. The criterion in this regard was always the adequacy of the information immediately available on relief cases from existing municipal records. Where municipalities had made reregistrations of
their relief recipients just immediately before the inception of the dominion classification, further reregistrations were unnecessary. Some municipalities periodically reregister relief recipients, and in many instances such local authorities collected the information required by the department at the next reregistration.
A third group of municipalities had partial information, and the deficiencies have been or are being met by securing further details from the relief recipients. The fourth and perhaps the largest group of municipalities have undertaken a reregistration of relief recipients in order to give their records a degree of uniformity with the rest of the country. It should be remembered that in all instances the provinces and municipalities have undertaken to cooperate with the Department of Labour in the securing of the requisite data.

speechtext: Is this information to be secured by the federal or the provincial and municipal authorities?

speechtext:
The actual information is being secured by the municipal and provincial authorities, but upon the basis of forms supplied by the federal Department of Labour. It might be observed that nearly four thousand local authorities are distributing relief through the nine provinces, and are furnishing us with the requisite information. The federal authorities distributing direct relief have also been asked to cooperate in supplying information covering their cases on a basis comparable to that used by the provincial and municipal authorities. Under this heading would come the Department of National Defence in respect to the relief camps heretofore operated under that department; as well as under the parks branch of the Depart-of the Interior. There would be the Department of Indian Affairs in respect to the Indian population, the Department of Pensions and National Health in respect to certain war pensioners, and the Department of the Interior in respect to the Yukon and Northwest Territories.
The returns received by the Department of Labour to date have been ample to permit of some preliminary tabulations being made, and from the progress made it is anticipated that in the course of a few weeks it will be possible to commence making a regular monthly tabulation of all phases of the relief situation. I should point out at this stage that there is clearly a difficulty in the matter of the various provinces and municipalities accommodating themselves immediately to the new forms. At the same time we have been impressed by their desire to secure information for us and the results thus far obtained have

speechtext: Who expresses an opinion as to who is employable and who is not?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT RELIEF AND PROVISION FOR NATIONAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will refer to that in a few moments; it is a material question. Actually the opinion is expressed and the classification made by those who originally register the applicant for relief, which means the municipality; and I think we may say that under this definition of unemployable the criterion is physical or mental unfitness. There are those who contend, with some ground I think, that a long period of idleness, or advancing age, may produce a condition of unemployability, and it will be desirable as we go along to try to find some more precise definition of unemployability, something that will possibly go beyond the very obvious criterion of physical and mental unfitness. It is not an easy problem to solve. You find very marked unemployment in the age group of sixty to seventy. It is very questionable whether many in that age group are going to be reemployed, and that does raise at least a question as to the attitude that should be adopted in relation to the higher age groups: whether, for example, we may not have to consider the problems of certain age groups as being somewhat different from those of other age groups. I simply suggest to my hon. friend now that the information supplied as to unemployability comes directly from the municipalities, and the dominion has not sought to lay down any hard and fast definition. In many of these matters it seems to me that as we gather this information and analyze it we shall be able to see our way more clearly. And that after all is the desired objective.

Now to return to the figures in respect to unemployment and relief. As revealed by these various tabulations it would appear that the large problem of unemployment and relief may be subdivided into three quite distinct sections, which may call for the application of different administrative and remedial policies over a period of years. First I would speak of the social problem of relief. Let me return to the total figures of those who are receiving assistance from the state because of either industrial unemployment or agricultural distress. This total figure for February is 1,310,423. That includes employables and unemployables with their dependents, together with those receiving relief in the drought areas of the wheat producing provinces, both heads of families and their dependents. That is the problem in its largest terms. This grand total of those receiving state assistance may be described as the social problem arising out of the existing economic situation. It has its origin in the elementary obligation of the state to provide for the subsistence of its members-to use the term employed by Jeremy Bentham-and who are in necessitous circumstances through no fault of their own. It is the political expression of the moral principle that we are members one of another and have duties towards our neighbours who are in distress. In our approach to this social problem we must be guided by a number of considerations which have been established in conscience or reason and confirmed by experience. We must for example see to it that a sufficiency of food and shelter and medical attention is provided for those who are in need.
And clothing.

Clothing obviously should be included. We must also ensure that our administrative organization for the relief of distress is developed to the highest possible point of efficiency and economy. In a federal state the obligation to care for those in necessitous circumstances rests upon a well established gradation of responsibility, involving
first the municipalities, then the provincial governments, and finally the dominion government when the problem of relief has assumed national dimensions. This division of responsibility in relation to relief requires clearly a very careful coordination of effort by governmental authorities and private welfare agencies, if waste and duplication are to be avoided and a reasonable service is to be rendered to those in need.
There is another consideration which must also be kept in mind as we approach the problem of unemployment and relief in its social aspect. I have suggested that a sufficiency of food and shelter, clothing and medical attention must be provided for those in need. That is not in dispute. In making this provision, however, there is equally an obligation upon governments to see that the arrangements for relief do not encourage the acceptance of voluntary idleness by relief recipients, or permit employers of labour to transfer to the state their obligation to pay a living wage but to conduct their operations with a due sense of social responsibility. I mention that here because some cases have been brought to my attention of employers of labour who have taken advantage of the existing situation and have paid wages upon so low a scale that those receiving those wages were receiving less than they would obtain if they were on relief. And I know it has been the practice in some municipalities to pay part time relief to some of those whose wages fall below the relief scale. Obviously such a situation is intolerable. It does seem to me that if on investigation we find an employer of labour who is taking advantage of this situation, we as a government are entitled to use the weapon of publicity to the fullest possible extent in order to brand that policy as high treason to the state in a time of great emergency. I grant you it should be done only after careful investigation. I have not referred this afternoon to the names of any employers, and I do not do so because I realize that even though the information may have been given to me in good faith it would not be fair to those employers to make the charge until I am fully satisfied as to its validity.
Finally it must be borne in mind that the relief of distress rests upon practical considerations as well as upon a moral obligation which has been assumed by the state as an association for the promotion of human welfare. The greatest resource of any country consists of its workers with hand and brain. This in the ultimate analysis is the true wealth of nations. Upon its labouring population the state depends for its productivity and its

Employment Commission-Mr. Rogers
real income in terms of goods and services. This is a truism, but we must not ignore its implications because it is so familiar and selfevident. It is to the interest of the state, quite apart from the question of obligation, to preserve the health and vigor of its people and as far as possible to prevent the impairment of the technical skill and efficiency of its workers. The provision of unemployment relief has been and is now a heavy financial burden, but any failure on our part to bear this burden would be tantamount to the wasting of an estate by a life tenant, and would mean irreparable injury to those who will inherit from us in years to come. In any long range view of governmental policy a just and reasonable provision of unemployment relief is a measure for the conservation of the human resources of the nation. All of us want our relief administration to come to an end as soon as possible. We realize that it must be surrounded by safeguards, but let us not forget that in its essential character it partakes of a policy of national conservation.
Apart from the provision of subsistence for those who suffer from involuntary unemployment, the social problem of relief calls for the careful segregation of unemployables from employables, and the formulation of special measures to deal with those who will no longer be able to work, even when work becomes available. I believe it is clear from our examination of this social aspect of the wider problem of unemployment and relief that there is a clear necessity resting upon us to study and analyze it along the lines I have indicated, in order that we may develop the appropriate long term measures to deal with it in its various aspects.
So much for the social problem of unemployment and relief. I have dealt with it inadequately. I do not wish to weary the house with a discussion of the problem, and there will be ample opportunity to develop some of these features when the house is in committee.
I pass now to what may be described as the economic problem of relief. Let me turn to the total figure of adult employables now in receipt of relief. In this connection I find the figure of 332,180 for January, subdivided as follows: Heads of families, 174,618; employable dependents, 104,229 and individual cases, 53,333. Are we not justified in saying that this figure of employables on relief represents the measure of the economic problem, as distinguished from the social problem? I use those terms for reasons which I believe will become apparent upon reflection or examination. If work can be found for employable heads of families now on relief we would no

longer have to be concerned with the provision of state assistance for their dependents. If in addition, or concurrently, work can be found for the individual employables the economic aspect of the relief problem will be under effective control.
Once more I should like to introduce a matter which may not be quite in line with what I have just been saying. It seems to me that if we are to induce a proper attitude towards this newer problem, so far as possible we should dispense with the relief figures running into millions in our discussion of unemployment. The relief problem is not an economic problem, but obviously a social one. It is also a problem of public finance. The economic problem is more manageable, and we should face it with the clear understanding that it is manageable.

The first proposition is subject to one limitation. It does not follow that dependents may not have to have relief because the heads of families have secured work. The position would depend entirely on the age of the dependents.

Yes, that is correct. But I am sure my right hon. friend will agree with me when I say that if it is possible to secure employment for the heads of families such employment should to a great extent bring about a liquidation of the problem of supplying relief for their dependents.

Depending on how much is going to be paid. If it is to be on a relief basis it again involves the question of how we are to give a proper standard for a family, and also the other question mentioned by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) during the campaign, namely sustenance for children. I do not see anything in the bill about this latter point. I was going to ask if anything along those lines had been in contemplation and if we were going to assume responsibility for the children of the nation whose parents are not able to take care of them. I thought the promise to care for children was the most commendable feature of the right hon. gentleman's appeal during the last election campaign.
No doubt the hon. member is aware that the actual determination of relief scales lies with the provinces and municipalities.
Yes, they have had control of relief administration and fixed relief allowance upon a purely emergency basis.

Unquestionably this is a matter which will require further study, When we think of the economic problem it is self-evident that the only satisfactory

Employment Commission-Mr. Rogers
and permanent cure for unemployment is employment. It is equally clear that there are only two kinds of employment, namely private and public. Public employment is directly under the control of governments, but is subject to the limitations imposed by the mechanism of public finance. Private employment is not directly under the control of governments but is affected, nevertheless, by conditions which may be created by government policy.
When we ask ourselves how we should approach the economic problem it seems to me it is evident that short range and long range measures will have to be applied. It is our view that if we are to secure a proper revival of industry in Canada it must be upon the basis of trade policies which will permit a more satisfactory exchange between this and other countries. It is our further view that the secondary industries in Canada are based essentially upon the prosperity and welfare of our great primary industries. This government has already given indication of its determination to wTork out a policy of that type, having faith that in due course it will not only assist the primary industries but create a home market in the only sense in which a home market ever exists in Canada, namely by placing purchasing power in the great agricultural areas of Canada, where the potential market for the secondary industries exists. It is not a case of pitting the secondary industries against the primary industries, and of suggesting that these must always be in opposition. Rather it is a question of finding, by experience with and examination of the true interests of Canada how it may be possible to reconcile the true interests of the primary industries and the legitimate interests of the secondary industries.
I believe it is useless for us to repair the superstructure of our economic life, as represented by our secondary industries, if its foundation as represented by our primary industries is crumbling away. I am not going to speak at length as to what may be done by public employment to meet the economic problem to which I have referred. I may state however that I am quite sure it has been proved by the experience of all countries that public employment of itself is not a solution. I repeat, it is not a solution. It would cost this country somewhere between $300,000,000 and $400,000,000 to put at work the employables in the category to which I have just referred.
Per annum?

Yes, per annum. It is
conceivable that this country might pursue a
policy of that kind this year and the year after, but it is not conceivable that this or any other country could continue a policy of that kind without adopting with all its implications the philosophy of socialism. None of us can see the shape of events to come; it is beyond our powers to know the direction in which we are ultimately tending, but this we do know, that the electorate of Canada is not prepared at the present time to accept a socialist state. We are under an obligation to preserve the foundations of the state as we have it to-day, recognizing at the same time our obligation to provide the maximum of human welfare for those who are members of the state. But surely in our whole attitude toward the provision of relief works, towards the creation of public employment as a solution of this problem, we must remember not only that we are dealing with a situation which exists to-day, but that we are trustees for a nation which has a to-morrow. If in dealing with this situation we, under the insistent demands of the present, are forgetful of cur duty to those who will inherit from us in time to come, I think we shall be unworthy of the confidence reposed in us by the Canadian electorate.
This then should mean that it is the duty of this government, as it is of any government, to try to find the means of using public works for the provision of relief so far as that is possible and reasonable, and at the same time to stimulate private employment by every means within our power. Upon the basis of the improvement that has taken place, upon the basis of the cooperation which I believe can be achieved through the instrumentality of a national employment commission, I believe that we may continue to make steady progress along the lines I have indicated and do so without at the same time impairing the foundations of our economic life. Apart altogether from the question whether sufficient public employment can be created to take up the slack, there is another question whether we are going to develop through government policy an attitude of complete dependence upon the state for the provision of employment. I suggest that upon the basis of the experience that we have had thus far with relief works we are not justified in assuming that the provision of such works upon a large scale would under present conditions produce that amount of human motivation which would make for the maximum efficiency.

Does the minister
believe that private industry will be able to absorb all the unemployed who are employable?

Employment Commission-Mr. Rogers

I do not think I have said that. If I might answer my hon. friend now I should like to put to him something which I had intended to refer to a little later. We sometimes forget that this world has passed through depressions before. It is well to remember that the world has passed through very serious crises before. I cannot help feeling that in that resolution there is embodied what might be regarded as the quick centre of our whole problem. From that quick centre and surrounding it there has grown up this whole problem of unemployment and all that that entails. When we deal, as we must perforce deal, with the question of youth reestablishment, we come to the quick centre of this whole great question.
It cannot help being disappointing to those of our youth who have had some definite hope of the government taking immediate action on their behalf to find that they have been relegated to a comparatively small part of a bill which serves to set up a national employment commission. If we turn to page 912 of Hansard of March 9 of this year

we shall find a speech by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail). The hon. member quoted briefly from a letter written to her by a mother who found herself unable to make ends meet after her children had reached an age when she could no longer receive mothers' allowance. This mother reported that her four children were now earning S3, SI.50, SI and $1 repectively per week, a total of $8.50, upon which she was no longer able to carry on as she had been when receiving mothers' allowance. As far as the morale of youth is concerned, we find here another serious condition. Those who are close to this whole great problem realize the stringent effect that there is upon youth at a time, as has been mentioned already in this chamber, when idleness is so prevalent throughout all parts of the country. An article in the Toronto Telegram of Tuesday, March 24, stated that in the last seven years crime among youth had doubled. Then, in some ways most important of all is the peculiar process of thought which has seemed to rob youth of its desire to learn. It is true that registrations at schools and universities are high, but I speak from no small experience when I say that there are those attending school to-day simply because they have nothing else to do. They say, "What are we going to do when we get through?" That attitude is not to be found only among the young men and young women; the same attitude of despair is to be found among the parents who themselves have experienced all the vicissitudes that accompany prolonged unemployment.
During the course of the debate upon the resolution to which I referred a few moments ago, mention was made of the possibility of using correspondence courses, national scholarships, reforestation schemes, apprenticeships and other methods which might be regarded as productive means of reestablishing youth. Let me mention also, if I may, how highly desirable it seems to me to be that the young man and young woman should have some place or someone to go to for advice. I am not minimizing in any way the efficiency of those who are in charge of our educational institutions; I am not minimizing for a moment the efficiency of those responsible for the conduct of our religious institutions, rather do I regard their efficiency highly, but who is better equipped to give the young man or young woman practical advice than someone who has gone through an experience such as that through which the youth in question is passing? Those of us who have had associations with both industrial

work and the work among young people realize how frequently advice is sought and the premise upon which such advice is sought. Will a member of a subcommittee of the commission or its representative in a locality be adequate to take care of this major phase of the problem?
It seems to me that there is much that the Minister of Labour can do immediately. He knows that certain and definite recommendations are going to be made by this commission. He must know there is that which is essentially obvious and which will be brought down in the report of this commission, but it will be a matter of weeks before the commission swings into action. It will be a matter of months before such an extended investigation can possibly be completed and a report made. One cannot help being disappointed when he realizes that after the many months that have gone by since October 14 and after the many weeks that we have sat here in parliament, only to-day are we considering a bill to set up an employment commission. I know the Minister of Labour will not feel I am criticizing this commission for what it may ultimately accomplish, but that I feel that the situation at the moment demands immediate action. Prior to October 14 we saw on the bill-boards throughout the length and breadth of this country-I am not speaking politically; I am speaking nationally-these words, "Vote Liberal and get action." People of this country voted Liberal. They got a Liberal government, but have they got action?
Yes.

Those who sit in the Liberal benches say "yes," but I wonder whether the man on the street will make the same reply. I wonder whether the man on the street who was on relief on October 14 and is still on relief will say that he voted Liberal and got action. I wonder whether the man who is on part time will say that he has got action. I wonder whether the young man or young woman who has nothing to do will say that he or she has got action. The government says that this takes time, but it is six months since the government was elected and we are now in the eighth week of the first session of a new parliament before this bill is brought down. I am not saying this merely as criticism-I prefaced my remarks with that statement-I am saying this because I feel there is much that can be done now. I am sure the minister feels that the trans-Canada highway can be completed, and I am sure he has heard what has been said in this chamber

with regard to the possibilities of employment through reforestation.
I repeat what I said before recess: The burden of this problem rests primarily with industry, and industry must be made conscious of that responsibility. I claim that there is little in this bill to make industry conscious of its responsibility. I have great confidence in the ability of the Minister of Labour. I listened patiently and with great interest this afternoon as he spoke when he disclosed a rare and intimate knowledge of the problem, both social and economic. I feel that he, having displayed that knowledge, can do much. Surely the Minister of Labour of the federal government is in a better position to act than is a commission which will take at least six months to bring in its report. Why not act now? Must we wait for this commission? The problem, I admit, is no longer an emergency-that is, the whole problem-for it has persisted since 1929, when it began. We listened this afternoon to an exposition of that phase of it showing that the situation has continued. It seems to me, speaking from some little knowledge of this matter, that whereas the immediate situation presents an emergency, the problem as a whole does not. We are told that normal unemployment in this country in the winter is 200,000. There is no longer any such thing as normal unemployment, and 200,000 cannot be regarded any longer as the normally unemployed. The man who is among these 200.000-and the same is true of the woman *-does not regard himself as being among the normally unemployed; the situation has passed that stage. We have educated the Canadian people to realize that as a government we recognize an unemployment situation. and therefore normal unemployment can no longer exist.
I think the crux of the -whole situation is simply this:	The people of Canada have
placed in this house the largest majority of members that ever supported a government in this dominion. We have heard from the benches to your right, Mr. Speaker, that the people have given this government a clear mandate. They have. They have confidence in this government, or better, they have said so. But will that confidence be retained unless action is taken? As a Canadian closely identified with those who earn their livelihood from industrial activities, and not without some knowledge of those who are dependent for their livelihood upon primary products, I earnestly urge upon the Minister of Labour that the time for action is now, and that he as Minister of Labour is better equipped to take action immediately than is
any commission which may swing into action some months from now.
The spirit of the bill, yes; I have applauded that. But as far as the immediate present is concerned, when those who are unemployed and on relief throughout the length and breadth of this country are looking to Ottawa, to parliament hill and to the office of the Minister of Labour, I say that action must begin in that quarter if public confidence is to be retained. Again let me congratulate the minister upon his knowledge of the whole subject and urge upon him if I may, as I take my seat, the necessity for himself as Minister of Labour setting in motion at once that which it is so vividly clear must be done.

I wish to offer my congratulations to the minister upon the presentation he made this afternoon; in my opinion he dealt in a masterly manner with a very difficult subject. In fact, the unemployment problem still remains the greatest question with which Canada has to deal; there is no doubt as to that.
I agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Massey) and with others who have spoken with regard to the plight of youth in Canada; that has been one of the most tragic features of the whole unemployment problem. Not many members, however, have had a word to say about the plight of youth in our agricultural districts, not because they are not all concerned with the welfare of the youth on our farms but for the reason, I think, that we farmers do not take much pride in our ability to express ourselves. I know something of the plight of youth in connection with agriculture, and as I cannot draw on my imagination-I am not saying this in disparagement of any hon. member-the remarks I have to make to-night will have to be from my actual experience with the people concerned. I have lived all my life with the youth and others on farms and I am in a position to know something about their actual condition.
I am sorry that perhaps the first words I have to utter to-night must be in criticism of the action recently taken by the government in increasing the allowance to the unemployed in the relief camps, not because I think they are getting too much but because in my opinion this is not going to work in the interests of Canada as a wffiole. I live on a farm which was bequeathed to me by my father and which is now occupied by my son in my absence. I hope the day will come when my grandsons will occupy that farm, and we are grimly hanging on to our heritage as thousands of other farmers in Canada are

doing. It is a tough job and many have fallen by the wayside. We have had poor crops, and we have had bountiful crops produced below cost of production; but withal we have had to pay high prices for our machinery; we have had to pay high interest rates pyramided from year to year, and on that account our taxation has been quite extreme and has almost forced us to leave the land.
Referring again to the money paid single unemployed in our camps, I do not think it was a good move on the part of the government, and I wish to give the house the actual experience of the men who are living close by and who know something about this great problem. I have received a protest from the rural council of Portage la Prairie against the increase in wages paid the men in the relief camps, and let me read a clipping from the Brandon Sun. It is a Conservative paper, but that does not hurt it in the least in this instance:
Many farm jobs available but no takers yet.
Single unemployed show no inclination to leave Shilo camp for farms.
Plenty of jobs are in sight for those who want them on farms, but so far the response has been anything but enthusiastic. Seventeen farm jobs are listed at the government employment bureau here, paying from $8 to $10 a month during seeding and increasing as the season advances. In the majority of cases the farmers want the men for the entire season and will sign contracts for that period.
Promises of $15 a month to the men in Shilo camp will probably cause a real shortage of farm labour this spring. The single men have shown no inclination to leave the camp, and with higher pay than they are being offered for farm work will probably stay at Shilo until such time as the new camp program is completed.

Will my hon. friend permit me to say a word on that point? Apart from the single homeless men in the relief camps, as he is perhaps aware, in Winnipeg, in Regina, in Edmonton and in Vancouver there are several thousands of single, homeless men who should be available for farm work if it is offered. That is to say, it is perhaps not quite fair to suggest that the farmers of western Canada are wholly dependent upon men in relief camps for agricultural assistance at this time.

It is perfectly true that there are lots of men still unemployed in our cities. But the fact that we have 20,000 in relief camps has a bearing upon the scarcity of farm labour; there is no doubt about that, and I do not think that, as long as they can get S15 a month and their tobacco, their clothes and their food, they will worry very much whether they go out on the land or not.

I mentioned in a previous debate that it costs $39 per month to keep each of these men in a relief camp. When you add the extra ten dollars which the government is granting, you have a cost of practically $50 a month to keep these men. I have stated before that these men could be placed out among the farmers at ten dollars to the man and ten dollars to the farmer, making $20 a month, which would more than cut the cost in half. I have practical experience in connection with conditions in western Canada, and I am inclined to think conditions all over the dominion are much the same. In any event I will read this letter, which I received from the province of Quebec:
Dear Mr. Leader,-
I have just read in the Hansard of 17th February, 1936, your very interesting speech on the solution of the unemployment problem.
Sir, I sincerely compliment you, here is a solution that is practical and full of promises on all sides.
$10 for the worker and $10 for the farmer to help defray the cost of workmen's board. Here is an ideal solution which will be interesting to everyone.
With these conditions, I am sure I can place at least 1,000 men in my community.
Perhaps I have said enough, and more than I intended, on this point. And now I should like to refer briefly to the reestablishment of agriculture, the rehabilitation of agriculture, as it is sometimes termed. I am glad that this bill provides a way whereby we can invite people to get back to the land which they have had to leave. We have had various land schemes in this country. I am not going to mention any of them to-night. They have operated with varying success; some are making good. In my opinion the greatest drawback with regard to these land schemes is that there is nothing permanent about the proposition. Those who participate are not placed in a position which will enable them to get title to the land, thereby giving them a sense of security and an incentive to build up a home, rear their families and remain independent, perhaps to the extent of not making them desirous of old age pensions when they reach the age of seventy. What we need in Canada are happy homes where people are contented and willing to use their best efforts to make a living. During the election I had the privilege of speaking over the radio. I dealt with what I called the back to the land movement. I believe that we must make farm life more attractive if we are going to get people to stay on the land. Allow me to read an extract from this speech, which was delivered at that time:
We all know, and no one better than those who are engaged in farm work, that farm life is not so attractive as city life. Farm homes

generally lack the modern convenience found so universally in the city. Although Canada has an abundance of electrical energy to meet the requirements of all its citizens, our governments have not yet been able to place this power within the reach of the farmer's pocketbook. This is one reason why our young farmers, both boys and girls, prefer a doubtful existence in the city to the more permanent though humdrum life on the farm. These young people should be retained on the land otherwise they will displace workers in the city. So it seems to me that our primary task should be to make rural habitation more attractive and less burdensome. This could be done in a large measure if our governing bodies would undertake to supply farmers with electrical energy and not limit the benefits of this modern labour-saving device to those residing in our towns and cities. Why should not farm women have the same opportunities as their sisters in the city and simply by the pressing of an electric button be relieved of much of the drudgery of housekeeping. I maintain that the invonceniences that we find so often in our farm homes have resulted in many rural families moving off the land and into the cities where they hope to enjoy life more abundantly.
During the election campaign the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) mentioned, though I think quite briefly, in one of his radio addresses the possibility of developing our electric power so that it would be able to take care of the needs of the rural districts. I thought this was a splendid feature of his address, and I hope that the time will come when the government of Manitoba, in common with the governments of the other provinces, will undertake this great work for our rural people.
I want briefly to allude to two conditions that exist in western Canada. We have in this country, and more particularly in the prairie provinces, thousands of ex-farmers and farm labourers in our towns and cities at the present time unemployed. Most of these men with their families are on relief. Many of these farmers, through no fault of their own were forced by circumstances to leave their farm homes. Others, perhaps, have failed on account of extravagant tastes that the farming business will not sustain, but whatever was the cause of their removal from the land most of these people would welcome the opportunity once again to take up their occupations as independent farmers. This I know from personal contact and observation.
Then we have in Canada and more particularly in the western provinces a large number of resident farmers who are cultivating too much land and who would be willing to part with some of their holdings even at the present low price of good farm lands. There are many farmers with a section of land or more that contain two or three sets of good buildings which are at present unoccupied. Speaking from experience again, I want to say that if you come out to my place I can take you to at least six farm homes, within a radius of two miles from where I live, that are vacant. Farmers own them; the lands are cultivated; they are working them, but they would be glad to sell those lands even at their present value. There, I think, is where the government could undertake to purchase such farm properties and get many of our farmers back on the land. Would it not be good business to reestablish farmers on the land containing these farm buildings, buying the land from the owner who by the sale might be relieved of a mortgage that at the present time covers the whole of his farmstead. This method of adjustment should meet with the approval of the mortgage companies who sometimes fail to grant the mortgagor any equity in his land. Any plan that would rehabilitate agriculture is in the nation's interest and should be cultivated by those who have the mandate to govern. And so we have thousands of these farmers looking for land and thousands of farms on which to place them. All we lack is a definite plan to take care of the situation, and it seems to me that this employment commission now being inaugurated by the government will be in a position to take care of the situation I have described. I notice that in eastern Canada people are thinking along the lines I have just indicated. I have a clipping from one of the Ottawa newspapers, I think it is the Ottawa Citizen, as follows:
Encourage men of experience to go back to the land
Welfare board in favour of farms radiating
from modern village for large settlement movements
This is an expression from eastern Canada:
Every encouragement should be given unemployed with previous experience in farming to return to the land with their families, the public welfare board decided yesterday when the whole problem of land settlement was discussed. It was thought, however, that the farming experience should not be too long past.
The community plan was favoured if the movement was a large one. The farm lands should radiate from a central village with modern conveniences and recreational facilities.
Such a movement, it was said, would be far too costly for any municipality to foster. Where individual families applied to go back on the land, however, it was felt that every encouragement should be given, if on examination of previous experience and work record, there was a good prospect of success.
At this point I want to emphasize that I would not encourage anyone to go on the land who was without practical experience and the will to make good. I want to read a letter I received from one of my constituents

Now I come back to the youth movement I mentioned a few moments ago. I say that

the first men we should try to take care of are the farmers' sons. There are no men in a better position to carry on the work of agriculture than are the boys who have grown up on the farms. We have thousands of farmers' sons in western Canada who have left the old farmsteads, not because there was not land available; probably their fathers had plenty of land, but they did not have the financial resources with which to establish the boys in homes of their own, so they drifted off into the cities. I say that our very first concern should be to maintain these farmers' sons on the land, because they will make the best farmers and the best citizens it would be possible to get. Thousands of these men have left the farms and gone to the cities, where they have displaced industrial workers. The very first man to secure a job in the cities is the farm lad. He is a man who will make good anywhere if he is given half a chance, but when he displaces a worker in the city he creates that much more unemployment. They do not want to go to the cities, I am satisfied of that; they would rather stay at home with their fathers, on farms of their own just across the road. They would rather marry their neighbours' daughters, settle down and establish homes on the land.
Then there is another class I should like to see looked after; I refer to the returned men. It has been said in this house that many of our returned men did not make good on the land because they were placed on land on which no one could make a living, and I believe that is true. According to the law at the present time if a returned man does not make good and owes the soldier settlement board money he is precluded from taking up any other land under the board by reason of being in debt. I say that this should be carefully investigated, and if a returned man is found who was not given a fair chance to make good he should be granted the privilege of starting over again on a better farm.
I should also like to look after the many farmers who left the land and went to the cities. It does not matter why they left, whether they were evicted or whether they were extravagant; at the present time many of these men are desirous of getting back home again. They want to get on the farm and have a chance to make a living. That is another class I would look after.
Then I know from personal experience that we have many so-called hired men in this country who have lived on farms for years and years, working for our very best farmers. These men are quite capable of taking hold of farms of their own and making good. Thousands of these men are in towns and cities,

This scheme which I have outlined could be undertaken by this employment commission. This is m line with the Prime Minister's declaration prior to the election, when he said, "This is too big a job for any one man.
