So I say, that there is no need for elaborate machinery for we already have machinery enough; all we want and ask for is the will to carry on the work.
Now, this money will have to be paid back; at least we think it should be paid back. Contrast the scheme of buying land at present values and getting these men back on the land with the schemes that have been in operation the last five years, of erecting great federal buildings at a cost of millions of dollars, every dollar of which was borrowed and on which we must pay interest in perpetuity. Contrast that with getting men on the land, getting title to the land and selling it to them at present values and giving them a chance to rehabilitate themselves. I say that it is not an expenditure which will never be realized on; the chances are that every dollar invested will be returned. There is where I say that we have to get down to hard pan. You have to get your feet on the ground- and consider what is in the best interests of this country.
Perhaps I am taking too much time. I will close with a few words in regard to my own district. The Portage district has been re

ferred to as the "fertile Portage plains"; it is one of the best, if not the best agricultural district in western Canada. Any hon. members who have visited that district will bear me out in that statement. But at present we are right up against it. In the midst of that
wonderful district is situated the city of Portage la Prairie with a population of 6,600, entirely dependent upon the prosperity of the surrounding district, and no one realizes this better than do the residents of that city. Let me give an illustration. In 1934 we had a wonderful crop on the Portage plains. We grow a lot of barley there, and the price was perhaps the best we ever received, seventy-five to eighty-five cents a bushel. The citizens of Portage la Prairie never had a better year. They got some of their old debts of five or six years standing, or even debts that were outlawed, paid off; it could be seen in the newspapers all over Canada that they had renewed prosperity. But last year it was a different story. Owing to the rust the crops were burnt in the fields and to-day Portage la Prairie is as flat as any city in Canada, notwithstanding that it is situated in one of our most fertile districts. In February we had the largest number of people on relief we ever had since the depression set in, 1,024 people, or one in six of the population, and the relief charges in February were 87,361.52.
These conditions must be remedied. This afternoon the Minister of Labour told us that the primary industries are the foundation upon which the secondary industries must be built. Our primary industry is agriculture and that is the foundation of the prosperity of Canada. Your superstructure will never last unless the foundation is solid. So what we must do at the earliest possible moment is to rehabilitate agriculture.

There are thousands of people to-day who have a great deal of money to invest; we all know that bank interest is low, as well as the interest on government bonds in which many people placed their savings for many years past, because they were getting nice interest. These people to-day are willing to put their money into any kind of investment, and will take a gamble if they are assured of stability. But the trouble is that there is no stability to-day on account of government interference. To-day everybody who has money to invest is under suspended sentence. They are afraid to put money into anything. The point I want to make is that if the government will keep from continually interfering with the business world this country will be restored to normalcy much faster than by some dreamy idea suggested in this house by hon. members on all sides.

should be encouraged rather than discouraged. If a commission is appointed in the present instance it will grow and grow and grow until there will be no end to it, and the expense in connection with carrying on its operations will be very heavy.
Then, we have a radio commission, another body which has grown extensively, and I say that any commission set up will develop in the same way. Hon. members elected to this House of Commons, especially those on the government side, should accept the responsibility of running the country. I, as a member elected by the people of my constituency, am willing to come here and accept my share of responsibility, even if I make mistakes. It is said that a man who does not make some mistakes does nothing, and I agree with the statement. I would rather have the government make mistakes in running the country than appoint commissions to run everything, because by such appointments the government shirks its responsibility. If the commissions appointed make recommendations which prove valuable the government takes the credit, and if the commissions are unsuccessful they are criticized, not the government. That is why they are appointed.
In the event of a commission being appointed in the present instance, who would be appointed? No doubt the government would appoint three or four good Liberal supporters; possibly they would include two or three professors from different high class colleges, men who are so full of education that they know nothing about business ethics. By such appointments we would get no further, in the end. My advice would be to let the minister do the work or, if he does

Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett
not care to do it himself, let him get some superman who could do it. I believe one man, assisted by the best help in the Departments of Labour and Immigration and Colonization, would do a better job than a commission would. I hope the idea of appointing a national commission will be dropped, so that we may have immediate action. Conditions are getting so serious, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) has said, that something must be done immediately. There is no need to wait another year; immediate action is needed.
Mr. A. MaeG. YOUNG (Saskatoon):	Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the minister upon the very able, and excellent presentation he made to the house this afternoon. Everyone recognizes that unemployment is one of the most serious problems in Canada to-day. I could speak for a long time to-night, but it is not my intention to say anything further. Mr. Speaker, I move the adjournment of the debate.

Mr. Speaker, I greatly regret that I have only now received papers which I desired at least to read before proceeding with my observations, but I shall endeavour to proceed as well as I can, under the circumstances, recognizing of course that the government has a majority to force the matter on in the way in which it has. I had thought this afternoon, of course, that they were going to conclude the debate. I asked for orders in council, because of a recital contained in the bill. I was informed this morning, when I telephoned, that there was no order in council but that there was an exchange of letters. I said that I would like to see them, but I am indebted to the chief whip of the Liberal party for within the last fifteen minutes giving me what I am told are the documents. But one of them is lacking; one of the documents referred to, of the few I did receive, is lacking; I refer to a telegram sent to Mr. Brouillette, who is president of the producers corporation.
I am very glad that the first minister is in his place, because I desire to make a few observations, which I hope will not be misunderstood, with respect to the second reading of the bill. We are told by the authorities that the second reading of a bill is the occasion on which the House of Commons debates the principle of the measure under consideration. The principle of the measure submitted to the consideration of the house is whether or not the Dominion of Canada shall take out of its consolidated revenue fund several millions of dollars for disbursement to members of pool organizations in western Canada. That is the principle. This could have been done by a short entry in the supplementary estimates, just as payments are being made to the harbour commissioners at Three Rivers, Halifax and Quebec. But the government desired to deal with it as a separate bill, and having dealt with it as a separate bill the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who has the measure in charge, spent some considerable time in reviewing the whole wheat situation of Canada from 1929-30 to to-day. While I think such a discussion is outside the principle involved in the second reading of the bill in question, the chair did not suggest that he should discontinue his observations, and I did not make any objection because I did not desire to be constantly raising questions of order.
I am in a real difficulty because twice in this house during the last few years I have at some length dealt with the whole problem as it presented itself to the Canadian people in 1930 and succeeding years. Last year I went to a great deal of trouble to get together vefy complete information with respect to the whole wheat situation as it affected Canada. Large numbers of figures were used; necessarily in transcribing them errors were made, and figures which had reference to one matter were put down as dealing with another. That is the position in unrevised Hansard from which the Minister of Agriculture read the other day. He stated, of course, that he was reading from unrevised Hansard. Had he taken the trouble to read from revised Hansard I think he would have had no trouble, or at least no difficulty in ascertaining that the figures to which I referred were figures which were absolutely correct. But one cannot always be certain that when using figures with great rapidity they will be correctly taken down, and in the hurry of not delaying the issue of Hansard sometimes they are misplaced.
I do not propose to deal at length with the whole wheat situation; I made up my
Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett

mind that I would not do so. But I am going to endeavour to deal with one or two matters, without taking up too much time. First of all I must point out that, as I have said, these matters were dealt with last year. I believe the revised Hansard of last year will contain sufficient for the purposes of my brief argument. The great care taken last year in dealing with this question was reflected by the mass of statistics placed upon Hansard. I think a perusal of these by any hon. gentleman who desires to be informed of the whole situation will satisfy him that although there may be the gravest differences between the then government and the present government as to how the problem should have been dealt with, there is no doubt as to what was done.

It will be seen that there has been a steady increase in the carry-over of wheat in this country from 1928-29 to date. That accumulated until at the end of July last year it was upwards of 200,000,000 bushels. Circumstances under which that carry-over accumulated and the increases occurred were stated very clearly last year and in very great detail. The causes that led to the increased accumulation may be said to be twofold:

Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett
First, the increase in the acreage in this country, and, second, the production of grain in large quantities by countries that had heretofore been largely importing or purely consuming countries.
The reason for the second factor is the fact that after the war the nations of the world that had to buy wheat made up their minds, first, that they would not be held to ransom because of their necessities and, second, that they dare not and could not face the possibilities of starvation incident to the destruction of wheat cargoes on the high seas. Therefore, we have in all European countries an increase in the acreage sown to wheat. I shall not pause to give them to-night because I gave them last year in very great detail, but this increase in acreage is reflected in the fact that France, Spain and Portugal are exporting wheat to the markets of the world. I recall the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) saying that he was greatly surprised that countries like Portugal and Spain should be exporters of wheat. I pointed out last year that Germany and France had at one time been great purchasers of wheat, but in one year they had produced more wheat than we had sold to them during recent years. I shall not again repeat the reasons except to say that I trust the house realizes that nations fearing war with its disturbed conditions were determined that they should not be dependent upon overseas supplies for the purpose of preventing their people from dying of starvation. Morocco, Algeria and northern Africa have made their contributions and every little corner of France and Germany has been cultivated. The Pontine marshes have been drained and Italy to-day is producing wheat in quantities never known before. These are facts that can be known to anyone who desires to investigate the figures available at the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, and the reports by the bureau of agriculture at Rome.
Then there was another factor that came into the picture, and that was Russia. In one year since 1930 Russia produced the enormous quantity of one billion bushels of wheat, a thousand million bushels. The production during some years in the intervening period has been lessened, and Russia at times has not been a factor in the world's market. But in that year Russia exported substantial quantities of wheat, and it is well known that in 1930 exports of wheat by Russia did much to demoralize the price of wheat in the buying markets of the world.
The other day reference was made to the production and consumption of wheat, and I 12739-103
pointed out the figures that will be found at page 3571 of revised Hansard, but which in the unrevised edition of Hansard are open to an entirely erroneous construction. I quote:
Mr. Bennett: The hon. member will see as I proceed. The average production of Europe (ex Russia) for the period 1923-24 to 1927-28 was 1,240,000,000 bushels. The average importations by importing countries for the same period were 601,000.000 bushels. The average consumption by European countries was 1.841.000,000 bushels. It will be observed that you have an average consumption during that period of 1,841.000.000 bushels. It has been stated that there has been a diminution in consumption but I give these figures to show that such is not the case. For the period 1929-30 to 1933-34-these are the crop years ending July 31-the average production of Europe (ex Russia) was 1,496,000,000 bushels. The average imports by importing countries for the same period had fallen from 601,000,000 bushels to 469,000,000 bushels while the average consumption had risen to 1,965,000,000 from

I stated then, as I state now, that there was an erroneous opinion abroad and in many sections of our country as well, that the people were consuming less wheat. The figures issued from Rome, and the figures issued as well by the wheat committee to which I shall presently refer, indicate that that was not the case and that consumption rose to the highest figure we have record of in history, namely,
2.123.000.	000 bushels by the countries to which I referred last year. Therefore it is not a question of underconsumption of wheat that produced the situation; it was the fact that there was a surplus of wheat relatively in the countries that had theretofore and heretofore been purely importing countries. In other words, they were supplying their own wants and having available substantial quantities to supply the wants of other parts of the world. I mention that because it was quite apparent from the observations made by the hon. gentleman that he desired to leave what I at least conceive to be an impression that was not in accordance with these facts. It may have been that it was because he was reading from unrevised Hansard, as he said he was, rather than from the figures contained in revised Hansard, which were in fact the figures I used in the house on the day on

Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett

which I brought this matter to the attention of the chamber. Thus we have, Mr. Speaker -and we might as well face it frankly-an overproduction which cannot be sold to the countries which in years gone by availed themselves of the opportunity to purchase the surplus of our production; in other words, while consumption has increased production has increased in consuming countries, so that they are able to take care of their own requirements to an extent that has never been the case before. Under these circumstances the abnormal carry-over of 1929, with the increased carry-over of 1930, created a situation that demanded action on the part of those charged with responsibility in connection with the government of the country.
Primarily the matter was one to be dealt with by the provinces inasmuch as their relation to the pools, to which reference was made on Friday last, was one of guarantors. In 1930 Mr. McFarland, about whom much has been said, went to England with the government delegation in connection with the meeting of the imperial conference. He went for the purpose of seeing what might be done to improve the situation with respect to our sales of wheat. He went to Liverpool and found cargoes of Russian wheat being offered for sale at a price that was less than would pay our growers to produce the article, to say nothing of transport to the sea and from the sea to Liverpool. That being so, the question arose as to what could be done to expand export of our wheat. From the information which we received it would appear that most of the nations of the world which had theretofore been consuming countries were now content to bonus the production of food to supply their own requirements, as I indicated a few moments ago; and even England at that time was contemplating entering upon a plan, which it has since adopted, of providing for bonuses for the production of wheat on a substantial scale.
The minister referred the other day to the fact that that year when Mr. McFarland came home he became the manager of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited. I should like to point out to the house the fact-it has been repeated so often that in my judgment it does not require restatement-that Mr. McFarland did not make known to me that he was becoming general manager of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, until h,e bad accepted! office. And I did not know he had done so until I returned to Canada; he had preceded: me.

He was employed by the directors of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, in November, 1930. The banks were anxious that the situation should be dealt with and, as I was subsequently informed1, the action of the banks, especially of the late Mr. Mc-Phail, resulted in Mr. McFarland's appointment and acceptance of office. He accepted office without reference to the government, without asking the government whether he should do so or not. Then they became aware of the fact that he had done so. Up to that point Mr. McFarland was the servant of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, which institution he served, as was pointed out, without reward.
When the next year came the situation was, as the minister has said, more difficult. In 1931 you had to deal not only with the accumulated surplus of the past but with the crop of that year, and naturally there was great anxiety on the part not only of those responsible for the marketing of the wheat, namely, the producers themselves, but of the managers of the various organizations, whether pool elevator companies or private enterprises. The premiers of the prairie provinces came to Ottawa and submitted their case for the creation of a wheat board and the fixing of a price for that season's crop. The government took the matter under careful consideration, and on July 10, 1931, the following letter was written by the then Prime Minister to each of the premiers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The letter addressed to Premier Brownlee read as follows:
My Dear Premier Brownlee,-
The cabinet has carefully considered the proposals made by the three western provinces to the effect that a wheat board should be established by the federal government for the purpose of handling the crop of 1931.
The government is of the opinion that under existing conditions the legal and other difficulties are such that no good purpose would be served by an endeavour being made by the government of Canada to enter into the business of marketing the grain crop of the year.
The governments of the three central provinces control a very large number of elevators, and those facilities will be available for the handling of this year's crop.
We suggest that representatives of the three provinces should meet together and undertake the formation of an ordinary trading corporation and that the elevotor facilities, over which the provincial governments have control, direct and indirect, should be leased to the corporation so formed for this season at least.	_
We further suggest that it is desirable, in view of the fact that the marketing of the wheat now owned by the pools in the three western provinces is under the direction of Mr. MARCH 30, 1936
Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett
John I. McFarland, that he should be the general manager of the new corporation. If this arrangement is satisfactory, the federal government will undertake to make the necessary financial arrangements to ensure the proper functioning of the corporation.
Yours faithfully,
(signed) R. B. Bennett.
It will be observed that in July, 1931, the marketing of the wheat then owned by the pools being under the direction of Mr. McFarland, it was suggested that if a corporation was formed he should be the new general manager. After much consideration that was regarded as being inadvisable, and shortly afterwards an arrangement was made by which the pools undertook to function as ordinary commercial enterprises, receiving grain and selling it if possible under the provisions of the guarantee which was given to them by the government and which was read in the house on Friday last.
The minister referred to the fact that there was a cut off. There was no cut off except in the sense in which it was clear that the business that was being carried on from that time, that is for the season of 1931, was being carried on on a different basis from what it had been before. For I shall presently refer to what took place in the committee that investigated these matters last year in the House of Commons, in order to make that point so certain that there can be no doubt as to the facts.
The crop of 1931 was harvested and marketed, and there was at that time in the hands of the cooperative producers something over 76,000.000 bushels of wheat, which was wheat that had been acquired by the pools, operating in the manner that has been described, as ordinary commercial enterprises, and with voluntary pooling if thought desirable-and many of them did so think-for the purpose of the cooperative effort still being maintained and continued. The net result of this was that stocks accumulated. Why? Because there was not an adequate market for our wheat. Now, there, differences of opinion will arise. Some will say that if we had endeavoured to force this wheat upon the market it would have been absorbed by the consuming countries. The evidence upon that point satisfies me, at least, that such would not have been the case. There is room for differences of opinion. But at any rate that is the fact; that there did accumulate in this country increasing quantities of wheat by reason of the surplus of 127,000,000 bushels as of July 31, 1930, being increased by the deficiencies in sales of the succeeding years' crops because, we say, not of lack of con-12739- 1034
sumptive power on the part of the countries that had hitherto purchased but because they did not desire, for the reason I have already given, to purchase wheat when they were supplying themselves with their own requirements.
It is quite true-and there need be no question about it-that during this time Mr. McFarland, while in the service of the crown, having been employed by Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, was empowered by the crown in the right of the dominion to stabilize so far as possible the wheat market. The reasons given for that have been ample and complete. There was no one to buy hedges. When the farmer hauled his wheat into the market place, whether it was at the elevator or at the siding for shipment over a platform, some one had to provide hedges, and unless the elevator companies, who are the primary purchasers, were able to secure hedges there could be no sale. For it is unnecessary, at least for me, to point out to the house that the amounts involved are so large that the capital of the elevator companies would not permit them with their own money to pay the purchase price for the wheat, but they must rely upon loans made from the banks, secured under the provisions of section 88 of the Bank Act, and the banks require that those who thus buy wheat and borrow money from them shall secure the banks against loss by a hedge. There was no one left but the government to take the hedges. And I desire here to point out that the government did not set up a new organization to deal with the hedging of wheat, but secured the consent of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, to deal with the matter of hedging supported by the guarantee of the government of Canada. There are no differences of opinion as to that. I do not know of any one, however bitter may be his partisanship, who has suggested any method by which the crops could be marketed unless some one was prepared to take the hedges. And I have neither seen nor heard any one suggest, in this house or out of it, that there was any one on the Winnipeg grain exchange to take the hedges. Some hon. members heard the evidence given last year and the excuses that were made as to why there was no one to take the hedges. But let us forget excuses; let us look at the facts. There was no one but the government of Canada, operating as I said through a guarantee given to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, managed by Mr. McFarland, to take the hedges. Has any one sug-
Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett

it, said that they did not see anything that could have been done under the circumstances other than what was done, because otherwise it meant complete and absolute ruin, chaos on a scale never before heard of. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Crerar), who is familiar with the operations that took place on the market in those days, must realize that if someone had not supported that market there would have been absolute and complete ruin, and the only "someone" to support that market was Mr. McFarland. We may argue as long as we have breath in our bodies; there will always be differences, acute differences of opinion, but the fact remains that unless someone had taken the speculative wheat thrown on the market in those days in July, an intolerable position in this country would have resulted. When it is said that he bought back the wheat which he sold, that is not a wholly erroneous statement. When it is said that he bought it back for less than he paid for it, that is the fact, but what was he to do if he was endeavouring to stabilize the position? That is Mr. McFarland's statement, and I leave it at that.
As regards the efforts to hold the market so that a bottom was maintained to prices, the statement that Mr. McFarland had increased the purchasing power of the farmers to the extent of $150,000,000 is merely an expression in concrete terms of the net result of stabilizing the price in the country at that time. It is said that it brought about sales resistance. Well, there are those of us who remember the editorials of the Winnipeg Free Press, when our bins were bursting with wheat and Argentine wheat was selling at a very low price, counselling us to hold our wheat because it must be required. That was counsel that was given by men who at least pretended to have wide knowledge and ripe experience in dealing with problems of this kind. Mr. McFarland believed that ultimately our Wheat would find for itself a place in the markets of the world. When that would be he could not say, but acting on the belief to which I have referred he took the action I have indicated.
What followed I am not going to traverse at all; it was dealt with last year by the committee; it will be dealt with again by a committee that has 'been set up to deal with the question of prices at Which wheat was sold and bought. I only remind the house of the fact that Colonel Ralston in this house placed upon Hansard a very complete review of the situation as he saw it, of what had been done in connection with the prices and the average

cost of the wheat and what it would be necessary for it to sell at in order that there might not be a loss. I will not take time to refer to that beyond saying that it was apparent that the wheat pools bought wheat in 1930 and made initial payments, as the minister has stated, of fifty cents a bushel in some cases, fifty-five cents a bushel in some cases and seventy cents in some cases. When prices rose they were constantly pressing that there should be recognition of the fact that their wheat was being held off the market.
In part of his speech the minister referred to the initial payment as the " set price " of seventy cents a bushel. Later on he made it clear that what was meant by " set price " was the initial payment made by the pools for wheat delivered to them. Starting out at seventy cents it fell to as low as fifty cents and even less than that in order that the margin of safety might be maintained. I will not traverse the reading of the reports of the Saskatchewan pools or others; I content myself with following up what I have already said as to what took place when last year it was desired that a wheat board should be set up to deal with the situation. I stated in this house that it was quite apparent that there was a general agreement that something had to be done. Even the most violently prejudiced witness from the grain exchange admitted that something had to be done, but the burden of their song was: Give us another chance; we feel quite certain that with another chance we shall be able to take care of hedges; they will not be left entirely to the government agency to deal with. However, as a result of the deliberations of the committee, the Canadian Wheat Board Act was finally passed by this house unanimously. The minister claimed in the speeches he made in 1930, to which I shall refer if I have time, that really it was a Liberal measure; that in its entirety it represented the views of the Liberal party. Well, what transpired with respect to it is very simple. A bill was introduced1 in the house providing for a compulsory pool, which would have had the effect of closing the grain exchange and putting the disposal of the crop in the hands of the board. Evidence was given, as I explained, at considerable length in the House of Commons committee by various witnesses who said that they thought they should 'have another chance. A witness from Vancouver said that they had built up through all these years a magnificent organization that should not be lightly scrapped; a witness from Winnipeg made a similar observation. In the end we compromised. We provided for a board, and provided that ordinary channels

Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett
that had been established for the marketing of grain should still be utilized for that purpose, but that a fixed price should be paid by the board, and if the farmers desired to sell to the private purchasers rather than to the board they could do so without difficulty. On that basis the act was passed unanimously.
I explained in the house at some length how we arrived at our conclusions. I need not trespass upon the time of the house to review that to-night ; if it becomes necessary to do so, it can be done later. But what happened was that the bill was reported back to the house, and, as I say, practically unanimously adopted, the only difference of opinion between the Liberal minority and the government majority finally being as to whether the act should continue in force until repealed or whether it should effect its own repeal by effluxion of time, and upon that point we took the view that it should remain in force until such time as it was repealed. Hence it stands in its present condition. There was also in the act a provision Whereby under order in council coarse grains could be brought within its operation, but that was not done. There was also provision for investigation of the grain exchange and for a clearing house; that was modified to some extent by the senate to provide that this should be done only with the consent of the governor in council. The measure, as finally amended, became the law of the country and was assented to in due course, and'-this is an amazing thing-for some strange reason the Liberal press of the west said that the act would never become operative, and advised the farmers to that effect, just as in 1932 when the imperial agreements were signed they advised the farmers that there was nothing in it with respect to hogs, and for a considerable time that market was lost.
Now, the position assumed is that because action was not taken promptly enough they sold some of their grain at a lesser price than the fixed price of 87i cents. It is an odd thing that always when opposition was thus urged against acts becoming effective, if it worked out so that the farmer got any benefit it was all the result of the prevision and prescience of the political party in question, but if on the other hand the farmers saw fit not to take advice, and to sell their wheat to the private purchasers, then of course, if they lost money because they sold for less than the fixed price, the blame must attach to the administration of the day.
The business of carrying forward the organization of the wheat board was done with as much expedition as possible, having regard to the fact that forms had to be
prepared and legal requirements met. My memory is that the house prorogued on July 5, and it was not until five weeks later, I believe, that the price was fixed.

September, was it? I thought it was August. I have not the date before me. and I never charged my memory with it. However I believe the minister is correct when he states that it was September. It was not until September, then, that the price was fixed. In the meantime Mr. Smith had come from London, because he had a very intimate knowledge of circumstances and conditions there, and had agreed to become a member of the board. Professor Grant of Winnipeg had also agreed to become a member of the board, and so, too, had Mr. McFarland. The fixing of the price, with the approval of the governor in council, was not an easy matter. There were those who would have fixed the price at one dollar. A great many of them believed wheat was bound to go to a dollar, at an early date. Then, there were those who would have fixed it at ninety cents, and others who believed that seventy-five cents was a reasonable price. Finally the government gave its approval to fixing the price at 87^ cents. That was the price at which the board was authorized to acquire the season's crop.
During the progress of debate, having regard to what transpired in the committee, some questions were asked regarding coarse grains. At page 4261 of Hansard, a question in committee by Colonel Ralston was answered by me as follows:
Mr. Bennett: As I said in committee, it is contemplated at the moment-of course what I say is subject to revision-that the board will take the place of the producers limited in connection with wheat but not in connection with other grains.
As a matter of fact there was no revision of that, and the bill finally passed the house and the senate, and was assented to without making provision for the board dealing in coarse grains.
There is in the act a provision by which under certain circumstances the act may be made applicable to coarse grains. That was never put into force, and in any event it has nothing to do with this matter, because it deals with coarse grains acquired in 1930 or thereabouts.
Let us look at the position from that moment forward. From that time on the board was purchasing wheat. It was also true that the pools were pressing to have a settlement in connection with what they

Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett
conceived to be their right not only to be reimbursed for coarse grains that had been sold, but also to have an adjustment for the wheat that had been held as stabilizing wheat upon a basis on which they said they might have sold it had they been operating, in the ordinary course of events, as sellers of wheat. They urged that strongly when the price of wheat rose; they did not urge it when the price of wheat was down.
The price of wheat went up and up, and in October, 1935, it had reached ninety-two and ninety-three cents at Fort William. In that regard it may be well to point out that the Free Press, to which the hon. member referred the other day, very properly appreciated the situation. Quoting from Mr. McLeod, and reading a few words from the Free Press, the minister pointed out that they realized the real reason pressure was being brought to bear in the situation was because there had been an increase in the price. At page 1549 of Hansard for the present session the hon. member reading from the Free Press of October 9, quoted as follows:
Upon the strength of the rising wheat prices the government stabilization agency (which is still doing business) would authorize the pool to issue cheques to pool members in adjustment of payments made on delivery of the crop in 1930-31.
That is the allegation made by the writer in the Free Press, and it is the correct statement of it. The pool took the position that they were entitled to settlement on the basis of this wheat being turned over to them because it could be sold at a profit. They did not desire to get ninety-three cents; they only regarded an adjustment on a sixty cent basis and, as he minister pointed out the other day, that would lave sufficient money to pay the carrying charges.

speechtext: Not at that time.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: Substantially, yes; thirty-three cents.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: Not in 1935; I pointed it out for 1933.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: In 1935 it would also pay the carrying charges, because those carrying charges had been reduced below the ordinary charges.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman is thinking about $1.05 a bushel.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: Not at the charges that were being paid. The charges being paid were ono-thirtieth of a cent a bushel, and last year it was reduced to one forty-fifth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: Just last year, that is all.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: And, I think, before that. However the hon. member says that is not so, and he has looked into it more than I have.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: I was not disputing the fact. But I assure my right hon. friend that carrying charges, inclusive of the period in which they were reduced, would have amounted to approximately $1.05.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext:
Yes; that figure is higher than the one concerning which I was informed. At any rate, they took that position.
Now, parliament had dealt with that matter. When parliament passed the Wheat Board Act discussion took place as to whether or not the wheat which had thus been utilized for stabilizing purposes should have been taken over by the wheat board. Finally, by the action not of the government, but of the committee and by the unanimous approval of the house, paragraph (f) of section 7 was accepted, and reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, to acquire-
That is, the board has power to acquire- -from Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, upon terms to be approved by the governor in council, all wheat or contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat in respect of which the government of Canada has given a guarantee.
That limited the power of the government, in that respect, to wheat, and the order in council was passed and was limited to wheat, and nothing but wheat. It was stated in the house that the power of the board to deal in the future was to be limited also to wheat, and not apply to coarse grain.
I have endeavoured to remember everything I could with respect to the matter, because I make it a rule that where documents have finally to be signed I do not charge my memory with the details, but let the documents speak for themselves as finally settled. If I had done otherwise I certainly would not have been able to survive the five years we held office. I never charged my mind with details when there were documents to be signed which, as finally agreed upon, would speak for themselves,
Now, what happened was this. I recall very definitely-the speech of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) brought some of it to my mind-that when I was in Montreal on either the eighth or ninth of October-[DOT] I could be sure by looking up the dates, but I have no memory as to just which it was- Mr. Paul Bredt, one of the directors of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, came and saw me there, and urged that this matter be disposed of. I gave him

Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett
to understand that we would pass an order in council to deal with the situation, and I asked one of my secretaries to come to Ottawa with him, as he did, and take up the matter with the two departments concerned, namely, the Department of Justice and the Department of Finance. There was no memorandum prepared by the minister. I felt clear that there was not. That reference in Mr. Rhodes' letter was to a memorandum from the Prime Minister's office when my secretary and Mr. Bredt had concluded their discussions in the Department of Justice. The order in council was thus completed. It then was taken and dealt with by the then Minister of Finance, the Hon. E. N. Rhodes. In the meantime I had gone to Toronto. That order in council provided for wheat and nothing else; under the terms of the statute to which I have just referred it could not refer to anything but wheat.
During the many interviews that the board of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, had with me they urged that inasmuch as their enterprise had been used for the purpose of stabilizing, they should receive something in their expense account for the utilization of their name and their facilities in carrying on these operations. I recall vividly at least two or three of them being in my room in the East block in the summer when this bill was before the house. I told them that this would have to stand until we found out whether they came out on the right side of the ledger, at which time it could be properly considered. I did not think it unfair that an organization that was already established, obviating the necessity of making any costly payments for the purposes of establishment, that was utilized as this one was for stabilization purposes, might receive something under certain contingencies.
I had no knowledge, nor had anyone round about Ottawa any knowledge as to the correctness or otherwise of the figures that were put forth. The letters were dictated by telephone, and the acceptance and offer made. The figures which Mr. Bredt had with him were filled in for the purpose of making the offer and acceptance. When the matter came to me at Toronto-I have no memory of this beyond what I am presently to say-I asked what was the warrant for these figures, and I was informed what the warrant was. There was no auditor's certificate; there was nothing to support them beyond the fact that they were stated to be the amounts. Whereupon I added the words that have been discussed so much in this house, and which provided that a certificate from the auditors
must be produced to verify the amounts to be paid. The provision to that effect in the order in council was not made by me; it was made in my absence and I did not see the order in council until after it was completed. The order in council provided in terms that there should be verification by auditors of the amounts before the sums stated should be paid.
In November last, after the election, I was out of the country for a substantial time when I found out what I am about to refer to. In the preamble of this bill it is stated definitely and positively that this wheat was taken over on the second day of December, 1935. Let us have no misunderstanding. Here are the words:
Whereas a transfer of wheat and contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat in respect of which the government of Canada had given a guarantee was made by Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited to the Canadian Wheat Board as of December 2, 1935, subject to final settlement of the terms of such transfer;
On Friday last I asked whether an order in council had been passed, and I was told that it had and it would be produced. I had not received it on Saturday, and this morning I telephoned to the secretary of the minister to request that it be sent to me. The minister was good enough to telephone himself and say that there was no order in council, but that there were letters. I said that I would like to have copies of the letters, but I did not receive them until a few moments before rising to speak. I am going to show to the house beyond all peradven-ture that this bill in its present form has no possible validity because it is based upon an absolute misstatement as to what are the facts. That is a serious statement to make. I have read that particular part of the preamble, and I am now going to read the correspondence which took place when I was far from here and of which I knew nothing until this afternoon. One of the communications is not here, and to this I shall presently refer. On November 12, 1935, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) wrote to Mr. McFarland of the Canadian Wheat Board, as follows:
Dear Mr. McFarland:
The committee of the cabinet appointed to deal with the wheat situation, regards it as desirable that the acquisition from the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, upon terms to be approved by the governor in council of "all wheat or contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat in respect of which the government of Canada has given a guarantee" be consummated immediately.
Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett

The order in council P.C. 3199 provides that the sum to be paid shall be verified by auditors' certificate. I enclose herewith copy of the order in council dated October 10, 1935.
The committee desires that the transfer take place at once in order to consolidate the whole situation, the amount to be paid to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited to be subject to the report of the auditors, which will be made at an early date.
Will you kindly proceed immediately with the matter.
Yours truly.
Then on November 18, 1935, is a letter from Mr. J. I. McFarland, Chief Commissioner of The Canadian Wheat Board at Winnipeg, to Hon. W. D. Euler, Minister of Trade and Commerce. It reads:
Dear Mr. Euler:
I am in receipt of your of November 12tli, together with copies of P.C. 3199 and other documents in connection therewith, all of which refers to the taking over by the wheat board of all wheat or contracts to purchase wheat now in the name of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited.
When I received your letter on Saturday, Mr. Brouillette, president of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, happened to be in the city and I took the matter up with him at once. He read over your letter and asked that I send copies of some to him at Regina as it would be necessary for him to call together his directors before he could give an answer on such an important matter.
In the meantime, please refer to the first paragraph of your letter which reads as follows:
The committee of the cabinet appointed to deal with the wheat situation, regards it as desirable that the acquisition from the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, upon terms to be approved by the governor in council of "All wheat or contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat in respect of which the ^government of Canada has given a guarantee ' be consummated immediately.
You will observe the quotation marks begin at the word "all'' and end with the word "guarantee," whereas it seems to me that probably your stenographer should have placed these quotation marks beginning with the word "upon." However, looking at it as it stands, it at once appeared to Mr. Brouillette as if the governor in council must again approve, notwithstanding the contents of P.C. 3199. It is not likely that he will have his directors together for some days, and it would expedite matters if you would advise me by wire whether that paragraph should read as follows:
The committee of the cabinet appointed to deal with the wheat situation, regards it as desirable that the acquisition from the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, "upon terms to be approved by the governor in council of all wheat or contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat in respect of which the government of Canada has given a guarantee" be consummated immediately.
I explained to Mr. Brouillette that what I believed your committee really desired was that this wheat or contracts to purchase wheat should be turned over to the board at the earliest possible date, by the government trans-
[Mr. Bennett.1
ferring its guarantee from the Canadian cooperative to the Canadian Wheat Board, and that furthermore it was your intention that the settlement of upwards of eight million dollars would be consummated when you had received from the auditors the certificates which Mr. Clark has requested from Price, Waterhouse and Company.
I may say that this is just what the wheat board would like to have arranged without delay and I can ee no reason why it would in any way prejudice the position of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, by handling the matter as you have suggested. However, no doubt they will be guided by their own lawyer, and just as soon as I have advice from them I will advise you. So that if they are agreeable we may then request the Minister of Finance to transfer the government's guarantee from Canadian wheat producers' account to the wheat board account at the same time as the officials of Canadian cooperative make a transfer of the wheat and wheat contracts.
Yours truly,
J. I. McFarland,
Chief Commissioner.
Immediately upon receipt of that letter, apparently, namely November 21, 1935, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) sent this telegram to Mr. McFarland:
Replying your letter November 18. As the amount properly payable to producers must necessarily be based upon report of auditors following their investigation now under way it follows that no assurance can be given that an amending order in council will not be necessary. Urge early action on my letter of November 12.
Then on the 22nd day of November, that is, the next day, Mr. McFarland addressed the following letter to the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
Dear Mr. Euler:
I received your message yesterday reading as follows: "Replying your letter November 18. As the amount properly payable to producers must necessarily be based upon report of auditors following their investigation now under way, it follows that no assurance can be given that an amending order in council will not be necessary. Urge early action on my letter of November 12."
I transmitted this message to the president of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, at Regina, by wire, and I have his acknowledgment in which he states that he will arrange for a meeting of their full board at the earliest possible date, and will submit the matter under discussion to them after which he will again communicate with me.
Under the circumstances there is nothing further this board can do until the producers company advise us the result of their deliberations. I can quite understand the opinion voiced in your message that until the auditors report lias been submitted there can be no assurance that an amending order in council will not be necessary. My experience in regard to the procedure necessary in matters of this

Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett
kind is limited but 1 would imagine if the auditors' certificate differs in any way from the amount of money mentioned in the order in council, it would be necessary to make an amendment thereto.
Yours truly,
J. I. McFarland,
Chief Commissioner.
Then there is a telegram from the Minister of Trade and Commerce to Mr. Brouillette, president of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, Regina, which purports to refer to another wire which he sent on the morning of December 4, which is not on the file and which I think I have a right to see because it is an integral part of this transaction.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will find, what I found, that the wire is out of order on the file. He will find it a little later on.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext:
It says:
No reply to my wire this morning having been received. 1 wish to advise further that we are determined in the public interest to demand the turning over of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers wheat to the wheat board forthwith. We would suggest that the best course of action you can pursue is to act on my letter of November 12th to Mr. McFarland in which I say that "the amount to be paid to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers. Limited, to be subject to the report of the auditors." Failing such action we shall be forced to invoke the powers conferred by order in council 974 of April 12, 1935. For your information we quote the relevant provisions-
"The governor in council may at any time fix and determine a date at which wheat producers shall proceed to sell and dispose of wheat and other grains in its possession and control,-and shall proceed to sell and dispose of all contracts for the future delivery to wheat producers of wheat and other grains." "Whenever wheat producers are required to proceed to sell and dispose of wheat and other grains and contracts, such sale and disposal shall be subject to any instructions that may be given from time to time by the Minister of Finance to wheat producers, as to quantities to be sold or disposed of and periods within which sale or disposal shall accordingly be effected."
In the final analysis it is always possible for the government to notify the banks that the guarantees will cease. While we have recited these alternatives we consider they should be unnecessary in the circumstances as it is obviously not reasonable that technicalities should be placed in the way of the execution of a policy determined upon by the government acting in the public interest.
W. D. Euler,
Minister of Trade and Commerce. (Copy sent to John I. McFarland, Manager Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, 4/12/35.)
Now the significance of that telegram is apparent to anyone. The Minister of Trade
and Commerce, being the minister named in the wheat board act, and not the Minister of Agriculture, tells the Canadian wheat producers that if they do not turn that wheat over one of two things may happen: "First, we will sell the wheat anyway, under the powers conferred on us by order in council; and second, we will cancel your guarantee with the banks". To that there seemed to be a fairly prompt response. On December 2, which was two days before that, Mr. McFarland had wired:
With further reference to your letter to me dated 12th November I have received from the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited the following letter "Upon being advised by you of the contents of Mr. Euler's letter of 12th November, 1935, I called a meeting of the board of directors of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited for the second day of December, 1935, at Winnipeg. At this meeting it was resolved to deliver to your board forthwith in terms of the contents of the order in council No. P.C. 3199, dated October 10, 1935, all wheat and contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat held by the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited. Auditors certificates verifying the amount to be paid by your board to Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited as required by the order in council above referred to were mailed to the Hon. E. N. Rhode the then Minister of Finance on October 15. 1935. Instructions have been issued to our officials to carry out delivery accordingly. Signed, L. C. Brouillette, president. Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited."
J. I. McFarland Chairman
Canadian Wheat Board
That is Mr. McFarland's telegram of December 2, which was two days before the message sent by the minister to Mr. Brouillette. Mr. Brouillette did not send this letter direct to Ottawa but sent it apparently to Mr. McFarland; but realizing its importance he telegraphed it through to bhe minister. For some reason the minister did not receive it, I judge, before he sent his telegram of December 4.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: The two of them crossed.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext:
Then we find the secretary of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, sending a telegram to Mr. Euler, Minister of Trade and Commerce:
Winnipeg, Manitoba, December 5, 1935.
Reference wire Mr. Brouillette assume this was filed prior to receipt my wire advising that transfer stocks, etc. under way. Canadian cooperative board anxious cooperate in completing transfer forthwith. Mr. Brouillette left Chicago this morning returning Regina. Please advise if in your opinion anything further we can do facilitate transfer.
F. W. Ransom Secretary
Canadian Cooperative Wheat
Producers, Limited
Wheat Board

Mr. Bennett

To that telegram on the same day, December 5, Mr. Euler, Minister of Trade and Commerce, sent a reply addressed to Mr. Ransom, reading:
Replying your wire of to-day. Pleased to note your desire to cooperate in completing transfer forthwith. Government of course desires to do full justice to producers. Can only suggest further that you agree to make transfer at once on basis of my letter November 12 to Mr. McFarland which does not prejudice your rights under order in council 3199. Kindly wire compliance.
W. D. Euler,
Minister of Trade and Commerce.
The next document is one which I think is of very considerable importance. It is stated to be an assignment and it reads:
In consideration of the mutual covenants and agreements contained in a certain agreement confirmed by order in council 3199, dated October 10, 1935, whereby the Canadian wheat board agreed to purchase and the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, agreed to sell its wheat stocks and contracts for the delivery of wheat:
We, the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, hereby assign absolutely to the Canadian wheat board all our right, title and interest in and to all wheat contracts to purchase or sell for future delivery carried upon our account with the Winnipeg Grain and Produce Exchange Clearing Association, together with all sums of money held by that association to our credit in the form of margins in connection therewith.
Dated at Winnipeg this 2nd day of December, 1935.
Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers,
Limited.
Per: F. W. Ransom,
Secretary.
And by telegraph on December 6, Mr. F. W. Ransom, secretary of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, wired the Minister of Trade and Commerce as follows: Reference wire yesterday stop We were advised complete agreement with your letter November twelve would alter our rights under order in council three one nine nine and as it seemed to us to be essential to maintain our position under that order in council at any rate until we had full information of nature and extent of any proposed changes in that position we sent our letter of December second and proceeded with delivery stop that advice had been confirmed stop We are calling executive meeting for Winnipeg Monday December ninth when we will endeavour find some formula to meet your suggestion of November twelve without altering rights under order in council stop Meantime to facilitate marketing operations we suggest that wheat board take delivery of any wheat or contracts which we hold and which the board find necessary or useful in its marketing operations without prejudice to the rights of ourselves the board or the government.
That was signed by F. W. Ransom, Secretary. He had already, on December 4, sent 
the following telegram to the Minister of Trade and Commerce:
Pursuant to instructions given Monday stocks are in process of delivery to board in terms of letter dated December second addressed to wheat board stop Your wire being forwarded to Mr. Brouillette who is out of city.
And on the fifth the minister wired Mr. Ransom:
Replying your wire of yesterday saying that stocks are in process of delivery to board on terms of letter dated December second addressed to wheat board would refer you to my night letter of yesterday which was filed before your wire as above was received.
Then follows on December 14 a most important communication:
Winnipeg, Man., Dec. 14, 1935. Hon. W. D. Euler,
Minister Trade and Commerce,
Ottawa, Ont.
Have today delivered to wheat board all stocks of wheat and contracts for delivery of wheat in our possession.
Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Ltd.
Copy sent to Mr. Murray, Mr. Gardiner, Mr. Crerar and Mr. Dunning.
And on December 17 the following telegram was sent by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, Winnipeg:
1 thank you for your wire of December fourteen stating that on that day you delivered to wheat board all stocks of wheat and contracts for delivery of wheat in your possession.
Copy sent to Mr. Murray, Mr. Gardiner, Mr. Crerar, and Mr. Dunning.
That is the correspondence that was furnished to me shortly before I rose in my place to deal with this matter. Now, sir, in the light of that correspondence-and I am sorry the first minister is not in his place -I ask this house how this preamble can possibly be justified. I have looked through the precedents with some care, and I find that there is no precedent for anything such as this. I ask men who value our institutions beyond considerations of mere party advantage to reflect upon this matter. Suppose, when an important matter that involved much acrimony was before this house some years ago, we had endeavoured to introduce a preamble such as this, what would have been thought of it? These things can always be done with a majority. But think of what this house has been led to believe, and then look at that correspondence. I leave the matter at that. Never in my little experience, nor in my reading, which has been rather extensive, have I known of the house being asked to take action upon the assumption that something was a fact and then, when

Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett
the bill was in its second reading stage, after the minister had presented it, correspondence was secured from him-with some reluctance, I am bound to say-which places the situation in an entirely different light.
Far be it from me to suggest that any one has deliberately deceived the house. But I ask the members-and after all none of them is so blinded by partisanship as to be wholly unfair at all times-if ever in their reading, their experience or their observation there was anything like this. It is now clear that this transaction was a completed one, completed on the 14th day of December; what is more, ratified by the government itself on the 17th, and further, that the instructions given by the Minister of Finance in connection with the audit were given for the very purpose of enabling him to secure the information asked for by the terms of the order in council of October last?
The Minister of Finance was good enough to furnish me this morning with a copy of the letter to which I have referred, that is, his letter dated the 5th day of November, 1935. It is important to remember that that is more than a month prior to the turning over of the wheat. The letter reads as follows:
1 have received from the chairman of the Canadian wheat board your report on "Equalization payments" in connection with the 1930 wheat pool. This report was submitted to us as your certificate required under the concluding paragraph of order in council P.C. 3199, dated October 10, 1935.
That document has not been produced.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: Yes, that one was produced. That is the one about which we have had all the controversy. Order in council P.C. 3199 is the document to which the right hon. gentleman added the words.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: That is not what I am talking about. Could anything be quite as offensive as that, Mr. Speaker? I am endeavouring to realize that I owe a duty to the future. As the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) this afternoon said, we in parliament are trustees; we have a view of the past, the present and the future, and I made up my mind that I would endeavour to present this case without heat. This house registers the answer that was given to my question.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: I think that is correct. The order in council mentioned is No. 3199.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: What I referred to was the statement by the minister that "I have received. . .your report on equalization payments in connection with the 1930 wheat pool," which report I have not seen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: Perhaps my right hon. friend has himself forgotten or was never aware of the fact that my predecessor in office received what apparently purported to be an auditor's report such as that called for, or to fill the demand of order in council P.C. 3199. My predecessor did not act upon that report. I examined it and found, as I state in that letter, that it apparently did not at all conform to the requirements of the order in council. I shall be very glad if it is relevant to bring it down, but inasmuch as it was a document not acted upon at all, either by my predecessor or myself, it did not occur to my mind as being necessary in this matter.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: Yes, I think that is a fair statement, because Mr. Brouillette, after the election, namely on October 15, sent a document to Mr. Rhodes, and the Minister of Finance now says that is the document to which he refers, and which has not been produced, as I can readily understand, because he did not regard it qs satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: I am quite sure that my right hon. friend would not, if he saw it.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext:
I am not questioning my hon. friend's statement. The letter continues:
I am attaching a copy of this order in council. You will note that the order authorized the Canadian wheat board to take over wheat and contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat from the Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, and to pay the sum of $8,262,415.37 "being the sum total of balances due to the primary producers, and expenses and other charges in connection with the holding and handling of the wheat," subject to this amount being "verified by auditors' certificates."
It is obvious that your report on "Equalization payments" does not in any sense meet the requirements of this order in council. It does not purport to show the sum total of balances due to primary producers and it includes payments to be made for coarse grain, whereas the order in council refers only to the sale to the board of wheat and contracts to purchase or take delivery of wheat.
There can be no stronger statement than that, from the government itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext: Quite.

maintopic: EQUALIZATION OF PAYMENTS WITH RESPECT TO 1930 WHEAT CROP
speechtext:
However, we understand, from discussion with your representative, Mr. K. Drennan, that your report was prepared before the order in council was passed and was obviously not intended by you to carry out the terms of the order in council, a copy of which you had not at that time seen.
As it is not possible for us to approve the implementing of the order in council without much more information than is now' available either in the departmental files or in the auditors' reports which have been submitted,
Wheat Board-Mr. Bennett

I desire you on behalf of the Department of Finance to make to us a complete report on the operations of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, in connection with the 1930 pool, with a view to giving us the facts necessary to determine "the amount due to primary producers" as required under the terms of the order in council.
Your report should include, in particular, the following:
(1)	General review in report form of the operations of the 1930 pool from its commencement until October 31, 1935.
(2)	Operating statements of the grain and contracts held for the 1930 pool, following through what happened to the grain originally taken over.
(3)	Operating statements of the stabilizing operations carried on by Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers under dominion government guarantee, explaining what relation, if any, these operations had to the 1930 pool account.
(4)	Detailed reports on the charges for carrying the grain and contracts, with explanatory comments as to each item, as to the allocation of costs between the 1930 pool account and the stabilization account and the justification of the procedure followed.
In brief, this department desires to have from you a full report with necessary supporting data relative to the situation arising from the operations of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, with special reference to what further payment, if any, is due to the primary producer as a result of those operations.
As you know, the board has also submitted to us reports from the auditors of the three provincial pools regarding certain expenses and charges of the provincial pools in connection with the 1930 crop. I wish you to consider and report upon what justification there may be for the payment of all or any of these items by the board, or whether, on the contrary, such expenses should not be deducted from any payment that might otherwise be due to primary producers.
I would appreciate it if you would immediately undertake this investigation and submit your report at the earliest possible date.
I am quite sure that the pool authorities and the board authorities will afford you every facility on presentation of this letter.
Yours faithfully,
(Signed) C. A. Dunning. Price, Waterhouse & Co.,
1105 Union Trust Building,
Winnipeg, Manitoba.

Now, let us proceed a step further. It is rather difficult to have to go over all this again, but I should like to refer to just one other matter. Once more I direct attention to the preamble. According to the authorities, in modern practice a preamble is unnecessary except in connection with a declaration of policy. You wall find one such preamble, for instance, in the bill having to do with the employment commission. These declarations of policy are set forth in this way, but when preambles get into the field of controversy, except in connection with private bills, they do not find their place in parliamentary enactments. This preamble bristles with inaccuracies, and unfortunately in the last few paragraphs statements have been made that could not be proven, for the reasons I have given. The rest of the preamble is, I think I can say without question

Mr. Gardiner also announced that the question of adjusting payments to farmers on the 1930-31 crop would be settled as quickly as it was possible. In that year initial pool payments were lowered so that some farmers got only 50 cents, others 55 cents, some 60 cents and some more. The plan was to give everyone at least 60 cents. This was the wheat on which an adjustment was to be made, but apparently there had been no agreement on it between Mr. McFarland and the pools till eight days before the general election.
The amount to be paid was $8,262,000 to make the average payment for the 76,000,000 bushels 60 cents a bushel. By order in council this was subject to certification by auditors. Auditors had been put to work, and as soon as they verified the matter the money would be paid.

With the limited number at our disposal we can only protest against a preamble such as that, which will be a blot upon the legislative action of this parliament for all time, which will constitute a precedent that I should hope will not be introduced in this house. Suppose when we were dealing with the legislation in connection with the Beauharnois transaction we had made the recitals which might have been made and which we could -with a majority have carried through parliament, what would you have thought of that, Mr. Speaker? I am not at all concerned with any personal feeling in the matter, but I am confident what the judgment of posterity will be upon it. About that I am certain.
There is one other matter with which I have to deal, and then I shall have concluded. The part that I could not understand of the hon. gentleman's speech was his continued asking why the profits arising from coarse grains had not been returned to the producers years ago. He said: The then government kept this money. That necessitates my making a statement of something which I think is clear from the orders in council, clear from the communications sent by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to Mr. McFarland. The government at no time have owned wheat; the bank account was carried on in the name of the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited. The very documents read by the minister indicate that the guarantees that were given were given to the banks on account of that organization. If anyone desires to ask the directors and managers why they did not make such payments, they are perfectly within their rights in doing so, because the directors and managers, not the government, had control over those amounts. But the government would of course be consulted about any action that was taken, in the very nature of things, but the government did not initiate, nor could it, because the government had given a guarantee and of course obviously before any action was taken the government would have to be asked to agree.
Then we go a step further.	This suggestion of the then government having control of these matters, which suggestion, as I say, ran through the hon. gentleman's speech, is entirely at variance with the facts, which are as I have indicated. One thing more remains to be said in respect of that. These gentlemen were urging that coarse grains should be considered. I do not know whether the minister meant Mr. Bredt; it may well be so, because he knew much more than I did. This was at Regina, and various other places, but obviously I felt myself bound by the provisions of the law, and I repeat to the house and to the country that anyone desiring for purely

political reasons to take the action suggested, would he have added the provision that there would have to be an auditor's certificate for the amount? That in itself indicates clearly, I think, what was in the mind of the government at that time. Not only that, but I do think-I do not know for sure, but I think that it may possibly be- that on the question of expenses something can be said for the claim constantly pressed that, after all, this organization was used for a period of years for the purpose of carrying on stabilizing operations. Mr. McFarland had served without pay as the manager of that enterprise, and the pressure, the pleading, the insistent suggestion that in the form of expenses they should get some reasonable allowance in that regard did not at any time seem to me unfair, provided of course that the operations had not resulted in a loss. He has referred at some length tj some observations made by myself with respect to limitation of acreage and similar problems involved in a decrease in production. He spoke very feelingly of this on Friday. Now, Mr. Speaker, it is correct that a wheat conference was held in London in 1933. It is true that at that conference there were represented practically all the nations interested in the wheat problem, and it is true that they arrived at certain conclusions. Saskatchewan was represented by its late attorney general, Mr. MacPherson, and on April 7, 1934, an act was passed by the legislature of Saskatchewan, entitled an act to confer certain powers relating to the control and marketing of wheat. That was a permissive act passed for the purpose of keeping faith with what had been done at London, and with respect to which the Manchester Guardian and other papers spoke very highly. Particularly did the Manchester Guardian, after reviewing the facts, refer to the situation in a manner which, I believe, in a few words summarizes the whole difficulty in connection with wheat:
But one surveys without hope the alternative -a continuing glut, added to each year by highly protected countries exporting a relatively small surplus, irrespective of cost and holding to ransom those better fitted to export but dependent upon exporting at a profit. If the wheat conference has saved the world from that madness, it has not laboured in vain.
That agreement was laid on the table and was signed by a large number of countries all, including Russia, interested in the wheat problem. Argentine gave an additional adherence, and the result was that Argentine forced sales upon the market, as explained before the committee last year, on terms which made the sale of our wheat difficult.
But, sir, in this house on Friday last the Minister of Agriculture spoke somewhat slightingly of what had been done; and, worse, he said that he wanted to know whether it was proposed or suggested that there should be any limitation with respect to acreage. It is well known that if a manufacturer finds there is no market for his product he ceases to produce in the volume in which he had produced. It is clear in all the reports we have received from day to day and from month to month with respect to work done in the United States and Canada that there is a lessening of the quantity which is being produced because the market is not there.
